Ahead of Ocarina of Time, Mario 64 was a learning moment for Miyamoto

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo has dropped another banger. The Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time Remake has arrived to fanfare almost matching the release of the 1998 original. But according to Shigeru Miyamoto, around the time that Link was coming face to face with the Great Deku Tree, Nintendo had been struggling to perfect the balance between innovation and execution.

Speaking to Keni Eno in 1996 (via Shmupulations), shortly after the release of Mario 64 and a couple of years before Ocarina of Time, Miyamoto was asked about the rising complexity and polish of Nintendo games, and whether he thought they should offer a sense of escapism. In response, he suggested that the fact Mario and Zelda games were being planned out at the same time meant that the "boundary" between the two franchises had "started to disappear."

Eno's comments focused heavily on the changes between pre-release and retail versions of Mario 64, but Miyamoto's answer was that while early demos might have felt a little more innovative, the polish of the retail version was better. However, "if you ask whether Nintendo should be satisfied as long as the commercial polish is high, I don't think so," he said. "There are two kinds of games - well-made games and interesting games - and the public perception of Nintendo's games has gradually shifted from 'interesting' to 'well-made'. We've ended up pouring a lot of our energy into that side of things."

Miyamoto said that with Mario 64 in the rear-view, Nintendo had "proven we can make a solid 3D action game. Because of that, I think we can aim for something more interesting next time."

It's not immediately clear what that 'next time' was supposed to be, but Nintendo's next big 3D action game would prove to be Ocarina of Time - a title that would prove to push the envelope in terms of both ambition and execution, securing all-timer status and a MetaCritic score of 99 that is unlikely to ever be meaningfully challenged. It would prove to be a highlight in an already-legendary run for Nintendo: Mario Kart 64 and Star Fox 64 launched in 1997, and Banjo-Kazooie, Pokemon Red/Blue, and F-Zero X would launch ahead of Ocarina in 1998, with Mario Party and Super Smash Bros following up in 1999.

But while the original launch of Ocarina of Time makes that balance between ambition and execution clear, the remake muddies the waters. While it's clear that Nintendo has done very well in delivering on its mission to recreate the game, can a remake ever capture the innovation of the original? And while the Switch 2 has given us the likes of Donkey Kong Bananza and Pokopia, it's also slipped a little with the more muted receptions around games like Mario Kart World and Pokemon Legends Z-A.

It's probably impossible to stay on the kind of winning run that Nintendo found itself in during the late 90s, but Miyamoto's assertion - that studios should strive to create games that are both ambitiously innovative and technically excellent - is something that I don't feel like I always see from the company in the mid-2020s. Ocarina of Time might remain a legendary release, but its remake is a reminder of just how much the industry has changed in the last three decades.

#3863. "I feel that sense of responsibility more acutely": After BioWare's closure, the makers of a new Mass Effect 3 co-op remaster mod look to carry their legacy

"It's like watching a friend lose a parent - maybe you're not attached, but you feel the secondhand distress"

It appears I was premature in suggesting that the closure of BioWare might quickly spell an end for Mass Effect 3's strangely good, preposterously enduring co-op mode. I reinstalled and logged on just last week, and easily found a series of packed lobbies. Still, it was always regrettable that 2021's Mass Effect Legendary Edition opted not to remaster this multiplayer component alongside its dolled-up main trilogy, thus failing to introduce to a new generation the joys of performing teleporting psychic headbutts as a millennia-old bipedal frog.

This oversight has now been addressed, with the release of the Legendary Edition Multiplayer mod for said remaster. It's both a reconstruction and a slight expansion of ME3 multi, built in secret since 2023 by the ME3Tweaks group: a modding collective who've previously imbued the Legendary Edition with Mass Effect 1's Pinnacle Station DLC. It's also, some of its makers tell me, a bittersweet expression of appreciation for a series that looks unlikely to continue after EA's Mass Effect 5 cancellation.

At least some of that affection can be seen in how Legendary Edition Multiplayer differs from the already-available LEMP mod, which uses AI vibecoding to slap a mechanically identical recreation of ME3's co-op into the Legendary Edition's ones and zeroes. ME3Tweaks's version instead adds, according to member and longtime ME modder Audemus, a "completely overhauled UI, rebaked level lighting, upscaled and redrawn textures, upgraded shaders, native LE features such as HDR and controller support, networking and server replication improvements, extensive bug fixes, and entirely new wave modes such as Unified and Coalition."

Unified mode, for instance, quite literally mixes up ME3's enemy factions by forming mishmashed waves of baddies from across the Geth, Reaper, and Cerberus armies, thereby dusting off and stamping on your 14-year-old battle tactics. The mod also offers the ability to use ME3Tweaks' own servers for matchmaking, though a private server option remains for scraps with mates.

I'll definitely be giving this a try, once I'm back from my current travels. Though as with those OG ME3 multiplayer sessions last week, it'll be with a certain glumness, knowing that – despite a vocal campaign to give Mass Effect 5 a reprieve– I'll be playing something that had its future cut short.

The circumstances aren't lost on Legendary Edition Multiplayer's creators. "BioWare's closure is an incredibly sad moment for the games industry, and a particularly heartbreaking thing for the Mass Effect fanbase to contend with," Audemus tells me over email. "I feel as though our responsibility as a modding community has always been to carry the torch for this franchise, with or without an official future for it. But now that the future of Mass Effect has never been more in question, I feel that sense of responsibility more acutely than I ever have before."

Mgamerz, another modder on the project, recalls how "The day BioWare closed it didn't hit me until later in the day, a sort of numbness I can't really describe. I've spent 14 years working on their games - it's like watching a friend lose a parent - maybe you're not attached, but you feel the secondhand distress."

For some Legendary Edition Multiplayer modders, the affected BioWare staff included developers they knew personally. ME3Tweaks had previously been invited to embargoed discussions with both BioWare and EA on game modding, and Mass Effect writer and director Mac Walters (who left BioWare voluntarily in 2023) allegedly advocated for an even closer relationship.

"It's a shame to see it shut down," Mgamerz says. "Everyone speculated about it, but I know from talking to people internally there, that nobody knew the guillotine was about to drop." [Owners EA say the decision was only made after "months of planning, review, and analysis", though independent reporting suggests it was largely down to a straight choice between making ME5 or Star Wars Battlefront 3.]

"When we had our NDA with BioWare (since expired), apparently Mac Walters pushed internally to get my dev team brought into the manifold," he adds. "I say this as 'apparently', cause due to scheduling issues we never got to speak with Mac. But secondhand stories tell me he was a big proponent of modders - something that I would have loved to see more publicly shown.

"It is disappointing to know that the people who helped build the world my work now builds upon were killed unceremoniously - a problem that plagues the industry, and what kept me from further pursuing entry into it, something I used to dream of doing when I was younger."

RPS lawyers are telling me to tell you that nobody was literally killed. All the same, and even as someone much more familiar with playing the Mass Effects than tinkering around in their engine bays, the ME3Tweaks team make relatable points: we can frolick around an uprezzed Firebase Hydro, biotically biffing half-robot Turians like it's 2012, but it'll be hard not to look at all those conspicuous waist-high walls and think about the people who put them there. The same's true of having your mind drift to thoughts of their successors.

But there's another way of looking at it, which is that mods like Legendary Edition Multiplayer can preserve and maintain an original developer's work well beyond what their leveraged-buyout executive overlords might deem financially inconvenient. "I hope," as Audemus puts it, "that this mod - along with the fact that we've been able to build the technology to make mods like this in the first place - sends a message that there is incredible value in this franchise, and a passionate fanbase that is not ready to say goodbye to this universe and these games."

#3862. Despite hardware worries and rising costs, Sony says PlayStation 6 development is on track and "progressing as scheduled"

Today, Thursday 5th November, 2026, Sony shared its latest financial results, reporting on the second quarter of financial year 2026 for the company. In a wide-ranging set of statements, we learned that the company's overall profits have been charged by the box office success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, and that its annual profit outlook has been raised following a particularly successful quarter.

As for PlayStation, Sony CFO Lin Tao hinted at the status of the PlayStation 6 - not yet named as such - which is currently being worked on in the company's gaming division. She noted that the console is "progressing as scheduled" and that staff are making "solid progress" on the machine (thanks, VGC). Tao also revealed that it's been a strong year for the PS5; total sales for the console have reached 97.9 million, thanks to a further 2.6 million sales throughout July, August and September 2026.

The most interesting bytes of information teased out of this call relate to Tao's claim that Sony has been able to offset the rise in memory costs via cost reductions and price increases, all helped by a yearly operating income boost of 89 percent. Sony notes that it has secured enough memory hardware for its next business year, which helps prepare the ground for PlayStation 6 production which should kick off in earnest next year.

"Although new PS5 unit sales are gradually declining as expected at this stage of the console life cycle, the PlayStation platform continues to expand and grow in a stable manner," Tao explained. "[Next year,] we intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform."

Tao outlines that Sony is beginning to pivot towards this new platform in terms of both investment and production, and that Sony will "attach great importance to a new platform and make the necessary investments for that." This platform - the as-yet-unofficially-named PS6 - will be announced "at an appropriate time in the future".

This all follows reports that the PS6's memory and storage alone reportedly cost more than $680, and that there is still no hard release date set for the console. In light of the fact that console manufacturing is being heavily impacted by the on-going component shortage, many are expecting the price of the base PS6 to be over $1000. We will have to see what Sony announces over the next year before we know for certain.

Here is an overview of the game, via its store pages:

Animals and people of Llama Town once lived side by side in harmony, a special bond that has since faded. It’s up to you as Llama Town’s new rancher to rekindle this forgotten connection! You’ll be raising generations of companions such as bunnies, capybaras, and horses, and running the adoption center to help them find loving homes. Which unique breeds will you discover? Who among the townsfolk will you befriend, marry, and maybe even start a family with?

Run Llama Town’s adoption center and bring the community back together one friendship at a time! Choose which of your animals are ready to meet their forever families, fulfill each resident’s personal adoption requests, and manage the center to make it a warm and welcoming space. Different residents connect with different companions depending on their personalities and traits, so finding the perfect match matters. Don’t worry, you’ll continue to see the critters you adopt out with their new families around town, so this isn’t goodbye!

Llama Town boasts a diverse and vibrant population for you to meet! From the bookish doctor to the rugged handyman, self-taught physicist, and aspiring designer, every resident has their own personality and story waiting to unfold. Forge new friendships and perhaps discover romance!

Challenge your friends to activities like jump rope, town cleaning, trivia games, spelling bees, and more! There’s never a dull moment in Llama Town!

The actor and food critic guides us through the games on his PC.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"

Dominic Armato is adventure game royalty, but an early adventure game experience almost killed his enthusiasm for videogames: "The one that really sticks in my head is The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy," he says. "It was just evil. I was a kid, and I'm trying to play this game that's one of the most difficult text adventure games ever written … It's not a happy memory. It's a miracle that I stuck with videogames at all."

Yet persist with games Armato did, becoming an avid fan of the point 'n' click adventures designed by LucasArts. This led Armato to audition for and be cast as mighty pirate Guybrush Threepwood for 1997's The Curse of Monkey Island. It's a role he would reprise for every subsequent Monkey Island game, including the remakes of The Secret of Monkey Island and Monkey Island 2, as well as 2022's excellent Return to Monkey Island.

Alongside Monkey Island Armato has appeared in games like Jedi Knight 2: Jedi Outcast and Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty. He's also an experienced dining critic, running his own food blog Skillet Doux until 2015, before working as a food writer for The Arizona Republic and the Phoenix New Times.

Armato is currently working on a new project, while also pondering a potential return to voice acting. "I'm trying to start doing voiceover for games again, so we'll see if I'm successful in that," he says. But he took a break from reviewing restaurants to show me around the grog-spattered tavern of his Steam library.

I am currently playing Chants of Sennaar. I've been doing a lot of flying, so I've been wearing out the Steam Deck lately. I was actually trying to start Silksong, but I screwed up and forgot to start it up once before I got on the plane, so I couldn't run it. I was like "Oh, crap, I gotta play something else!" So I picked up Chants of Sennaar instead and I got hooked into that.

I'm enjoying that one an awful lot. I dig those slow-paced puzzle games that have an idea. You get a little bit of a world. You get a little bit of a story in there. It's kind of atmospheric, and there's some good [mysteries] in there, and you can just live in them and solve puzzles for a while.

I very much enjoy that genre. I'm not really a genre gamer in general. I tend to pick and choose the real shining examples of each genre. But I would probably be lying if I didn't say I was maybe a little more drawn to that kind of game a lot of the time.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

I just finished replaying Control in preparation for the new one.

I'll play anything Remedy. I love Remedy so, so much, and with the new one coming out, I wanted to go back and replay the first one again. So now I'm primed and ready.

The feel of that game is so great. It's so unashamedly Twin Peaks meets X-Files meets brutalist architecture, which was weirdly right in my wheelhouse. I like all brutalist architecture, so I'm just happy walking through that space.

I've always enjoyed [Remedy's] games, but I really got obsessive about it with the last few installations. I loved Max Payne, I really enjoyed the original Alan Wake, and I certainly would have always said I liked their games. But those last two were absolutely phenomenal.

I don't mean to front here, because while I am an old school LucasArts fan big time—and I was even before I got to work with them—I've got to be honest, I'm still not clicking with Maniac. Every once in a while I will pick it up. I'll give it another shot and I get 10 minutes in and I'm like "Oh, this is tedious, man".

Maybe it's that old Hitchhiker's feeling again, where at some point I feel like I'm banging my head against the wall … I realise it's this important, seminal game in the LucasArts universe, and so much came out of that. But it has yet to click with me, and yet I still leave it on there because I feel compelled. It's like when you've got some food that just doesn't quite sit right with you, and you think 'I'm just gonna keep trying it, and maybe one day it will reveal its beauty to me'.

You can see the genesis, the root of that style. But it's in a phase of development where it is interesting, but it hasn't quite yet become entertaining. That's where it is for me. I find it fascinating, especially from a historical standpoint, but it's not quite entertaining for me yet.

I have potentially two here. Steam will tell you it's Red Dead Redemption 2 at 289.8 hours, which mostly makes sense because that was my COVID lockdown game. In a bit of fortuitous timing, in the fall of 2019 I had this moment where I thought, "You know what? My kids are pretty much grown up now. I have time for videogames now. I can maybe actually justify having a gaming rig again. I always was a PC gamer and switched to console when I had little kids."

So I built a big badass gaming PC right at the end of 2019. Three months later, it was like, "Well, OK then." I got the 32:9 monitor. I went huge with the whole thing. So basically, me for the lockdown, we're stuck in the house, and RDR2 was every day. Most of that 300 hours wasn't even playing the game. I would just get on a horse and ride.

Now, that's what Steam will tell you. But I am quite confident that I put far more hours into Thief: The Dark Project.

I played that game in an absolutely obsessive fashion, where I'd spend 15-20 hours completing a level. It should have gone through at least one full day/night cycle, but it's [always] nighttime in the game, and my rule was always that I wasn't allowed to do anything else until I had knocked out every single enemy on the level and stacked them all in one corner. Then I could explore and find absolutely everything without worrying about getting caught.

I played recently and I hadn't picked it up in a while—it had probably been like five or six years—and it comes back right away. The little leans, the half-creep across hard floors, the jerky thing you do to move across [metal] floors without making any noise.

It's getting a little old and creaky, and it's not quite as immersive as it used to be, but it's still close enough … even today, I can't think of any game that has nailed 3D sound in the way Thief did. Maybe there's some I haven't played, but I remember walking to some room and hid[ing] behind the bar, and you can hear exactly where the guard goes walking around the corner. You don't even need to see any of it to understand what's going on.

So that's one of my all-timers, and I'm absolutely certain that I put more time into that.

This is a weird one. You know when you have those bizarre little time-waster games that you don't have to put any brain power into whatsoever? Forbidden Island. It's just some dumb port of a tabletop game, and that's my "Oh I'm gonna sit down and have my lunch and I'll tap this on the side". So that's the one I think, I don't know what I'd do without that.

It's a great co-op tabletop game. When I play it on the PC, I just play all the characters myself. You know how that is. For my dad, it was Solitaire. Whatever Solitaire game was being sold on the computer, he'd take a break for a few minutes and play Solitaire. And that's like my thing. [To] rest my brain for a minute, I'll just play one game of Forbidden Island, and it takes 10 minutes and then I'll move on.

This is really bizarre, but it's a little utility called Klack, and it's one of those ones that pipes in mechanical keyboard noises when you're typing on a laptop PC.

I spent a number of years as a dining critic, and I wrote a lot and I missed the noise of a keyboard. I installed this app on my laptop so that I would have little mechanical keyboard noises as I type, and I swear to God it helps me write. I don't know why. It makes no sense whatsoever, but my writing flows easier when I've got that clackety clackety clack mechanical keyboard noise.

There was one point, not too long ago, where I turned it off for some reason, and then I went through a period of two or three weeks where I just felt like, "Man, I'm having a really hard time. The words aren't flowing. I'm really having a hard time writing this month." And then, all of a sudden, I realised, "Oh shit! I turned off Klack!" And it all started going out again.

It's the dumbest thing in the world, but I swear to God it works.

Extremely, and it really stresses me out when it's not. In real life, I tend to inspire a lot of clutter, but digitally I run a tight ship. On my gaming PC, the only thing that will be on my desktop is something game related, or my notes on that game, or my spreadsheet for that game, and that's it. Then as soon as I finish that game, I'll get rid of those, stick them in the archive, and start the next one. On a work machine, it's whatever I'm working on that day, as that's it.

[With] my files, I start with the six-digit date code—that's year, month, day—so they all autosort. [I have] every single photograph for the dining criticism work I do. I still have, photographed, every single menu, every single dish I've eaten for the past 15 years. I have the spreadsheet that has notes on every single restaurant dish I've eaten over the last 15 years … I'm up to 23,569 restaurant dishes right now. And actually, I'm running a little behind. I haven't updated it in a couple of weeks.

#3859. Path of Exile 2's 1.0 version is out this year after all, arriving in December with a full campaign, two neat new classes, and more

About a year ago, the devs behind Path of Exile 2 delayed the game's 1.0 release to an unspecified point in time, only offering the hope that it wouldn't slip into 2027 (doing much the same about half a year later). But there's good news: it won't! As the action RPG now has a 1.0 release date locked in, alongside a look at what you can expect when it arrives.

As shared by developer Grinding Gear Games, Path of Exile 2 will be launching into 1.0 next month on December 11th. Probably the biggest aspect of the update is the fact that the game's campaign will be completely playable, with the fifth and sixth acts being added in wrapping up the story that's been built up over its early access release. You'll also have two new classes to play around with, if you've gotten bored of the ones you've tried so far or just fancy something new.

The first is the Shadow, which appropriately introduces a stealth mechanic. As you might expect of such a class, while you're in stealth, "monsters can't see you until you get within a short distance of them." Being in said mode also bolsters your dagger with a range of bonuses, and the Shadow also has another weapon type available to them, traps. You prepare these in stealth, "then trigger them automatically as you strike. Traps explode in the order they were thrown, allowing you to set up the perfect combo!" And the other class is the Duelist, who has the new stance mechanic. This lets you strengthen your sword skills, "enhancing each of them in different ways," with various stances allowing for "even deadlier combinations."

Beyond that, there's a new league to try out that lets you team up with Varek and his mercs to "conquer Wraeclast!" A whole bunch of new items have been added in, with many being revamped, and you'll also find new skills gems and support gems reworked. The passive skill tree has also seen a makeover, and a number of classes have also received some improvements. You can read about all of that in more detail right here.

#3858. World of Warcraft: Forever is off to a great start with Blizzard's smoothest launch in memory

World of Warcraft: Forever came out last night. Those who stayed up were prepared for the usual from major WoW releases: long queues, disconnects, and server lag. However, save for a few minor hiccups here and there, things went off without a hitch.

Eurogamer can report first-hand that for European players who stayed up from, let's say 11pm - 3:50am last night, the login queues were short and constantly moving. Those who were very keen to get in the moment servers went live ran into unclickable server selection boxes, but backing out and re-joining the short queue fixed this problem swiftly.

Once you got in, there was very little server lag save for a lost spell cast or two, nor were constant random disconnects that would boot you out into the cold (I didn't get disconnected once - a record). As far as WoW launches go, an incredibly smooth first day.

This was acknowledged by World of Warcraft developers, such as executive producer Holly Longdale who wrote on X: "At the risk of jinxing things, so far so goodish which is crazy by itself. The team prepared a lot since the wildness of Beta. And this launch was crazier than the insanity we imagined but thankfully the team built plans and contingencies. They are incredible in my opinion.".

Josh "Aggrend" Greenfield, a senior game designer on World of Warcraft Forever, addressed some minor issues that did pop up. These include a zone population problem: in basic terms the megaservers split players into different shards, and some of these felt a bit empty of players. There was also a quirk with the various big boats and zeppelins dotted around the map, which were busted. Temporary portals were added to provide a workaround.

"Thanks for everyone making this a great, super smooth launch," Greenfield wrote. "I’m going to head home and 'go to sleep' now. Yep, sleeping. Totally not playing WoW Forever until 3am. Nope."

The reaction to this silky smooth launch has some players flabbergasted. "I can't believe how smooth this launch is" is the title of Reddit user Arizhela's post, currently topping the WoW Forever board. They continue: "I fully expected to not be able to play today, but I logged in with no queue and no lag."

Another post, created in the early hours of this morning, is dubbed: "Never take a day off for launch, they said" in which a WoW player regrets not booking some time off from work this week, expecting problems. "You've been finessed son," replied user SnooWalruses3948, while SirePuns shared in the shock: "The advice was sound, but this time around the developers hired a witch I tell you. The code must’ve been witchcraft, the hardware must’ve been blessed by a witch as well."

It is unclear just how well World of Warcraft: Forever's launch was, given the unsocialable and employment-averse release time in the dead of night for us Europeans, but it follows a record-breaking beta period in which many hopped back into the MMO. Impressions from this beta were largely positive, the magic of the old MMO seemingly recaptured.

#3857. "This trailer is my way of saying goodbye": Have a listen to the Mass Effect 5 score that could have been, courtesy of one of the original games' composers

By this point I'm probably safe in assuming that you all know EA are shutting down BioWare, and that Mass Effect 5 has been cancelled in turn. You may have also seen that an internal trailer for Mass Effect 5, or Universe as it was seemingly going to be called, was leaked not long after the news broke, and that Sam Hulick, one of the composers on the original trilogy of games, shared he was going to offer up his re-scored version of the trailer. Well, it's N7 Day, as rough as that will be for many of the developers on the game, but Hulick has stood by his word, and shared an oral glimpse at what the world of Mass Effect Universe could have sounded like.

You can check out this new version of the trailer below, perhaps pop it on while you have a read of the rest of this post, as Hulick did also write in a Patreon blog about his experience with the series. "As part of my own closure, and as a love letter to the fans, I really wanted to re-score the leaked Mass Effect Universe trailer in time for N7 Day this year," he wrote. "BioWare edited a killer track called “Quartz” by French 79 to fit their trailer, which I think hinted at a slight directional shift in the score. Using that as inspiration, along with the musical tone from my work on the first three Mass Effect games, I hit the studio and got to work."

As it turns out, BioWare had actually reached out to Hulick asking him to potentially do some work for the project. "This year, BioWare emailed me asking if I was interested in working with them on an internal demo, and they said they were 'hoping to get some music written that would feel like Mass [Effect], supporting our new direction.' Of course, I said yes!" This doesn't mean he wouldn't have composed the actual game, as a composer hadn't been officially selected, but Hulick said he was "more than happy to collaborate on the new game’s musical direction and help make their internal demo sound as good as it could."

Hulick also spoke of some of the ideas he had for the direction Mass Effect Universe's soundtrack could take, noting how he "thought it would’ve been incredible to bring more songs with lyrics into the game," considering how many people loved the first game's end-credits song. "This would’ve been a great way to highlight more emotional moments in the narrative. Artists at the top of my collaboration list included Gunship, NINA, and The Midnight, all of whom have a moody, cinematic synthwave vibe that would’ve meshed well with the score in my head. And I’m pretty sure the Gunship guys are gamers, and if they’re Mass Effect fans, that would’ve been the icing on the cake!"

Of course, with the studio now closing, this never got to go very far, the news hitting Hulick "particularly hard, as the Mass Effect trilogy is a core part of my origin story as a composer." For the composer, ultimately "this trailer is my way of saying goodbye… at least for now." This continues to be a horrendously sad moment in the industry! As always, solidarity with the team at BioWare.

#3856. PlayStation sees record high player numbers and increased revenue for Q2 2026, and a lot of that success is down to Marvel's Wolverine

As part of today's (Thursday 5th November, 2026) financial results, Sony has confirmed that monthly active users, referred to as MAU, across both PlayStation 4 and 5, reached 127 million in September. This represents a seven percent growth year-on-year for the company, and sets a new record high.

In Layman's terms, this simply means that more people are engaged with the PlayStation ecosystem now than ever before. And it's not just that there are more people using machines and occasionally booting up their consoles; active play time also increased over the past quarter, too, with total logged play time increasing by four percent, year-on-year. As a result, Sony and PlayStation noted that its Game & Network Services division saw revenue grow by nine percent year-on-year, resulting in operating profit rising by 83 percent year-on-year.

Notably, despite its mixed reception, Marvel's Wolverine was name-checked as a driving force for the decent performance over the past quarter - but that shouldn't be a surprise for anyone that's actually been paying attention to how the game performed. The game sold through 2.4 million copies as of 4th November (so, in roughly 50 days). Ghost of Yotei, meanwhile, has sold through 3.3 million since its launch in October 2025.

More people playing consoles, and for longer - it must all be good news for Sony right? Well, not all the graphs are showing growth. PS5 hardware sales continue to gradually decline: in the reporting period, Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 consoles, down from 4 million in the same quarter in 2025. But, with 100 million PS5 units out in the wild, and 127 million PlayStation accounts across the whole ecosystem, Sony doesn't seem that worried: instead, the company is now focusing on converting those with active accounts into more viable customers.

Elsewhere in the results, we heard from Sony CFO Lin Tao that the PlayStation 6 is on track and "progressing as scheduled", with "solid progress" expected on the machine in 2027. Regarding those falling PS5 sales, Tao also referenced that, and says it's all part of the natural cycle of console launches and iteration. "Although new PS5 unit sales are gradually declining as expected at this stage of the console life cycle, the PlayStation platform continues to expand and grow in a stable manner," Tao explained. "[Next year,] we intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform."

It must be encouraging for Sony to see this growth in this quarter, especially after all the bad press and furore around the company's decision to end the manufacturing of PlayStation discs by January 2028. It seems to be a core part of the gaming audience's understanding of game ownership, the decision has been widely contested as anti-consumer. It's caused a lot of bad blood with PlayStation players over the past six months, but - seemingly, given these results - that has translated to very little material impact on Sony's bottom line.

#3855. Beholder IV announced for PC

Alawar has announced Beholder IV, the latest installment in its dystopian narrative series, as part of the franchise’s 10th anniversary celebrations. It will be available for PC via Steam.

The announcement is accompanied by the release of the new digital comic, Beholder: The Landlord’s Handbook, and a 90 percent-off discount on the original Beholder.

Here is an overview of Beholder IV, via its Steam page:

From the creators of Beholder: Conductor.

Beholder IV returns to a totalitarian State where your choices matter. Live a double life as an official and underground agent. Spy, sabotage, build relationships, and decide others’ fates. But brace for a knock: the police are coming, and your home is full of evidence.

You used to watch your tenants, peer through keyholes, and report those who fell foul of the State. Now everything has changed.

You are a young Ministry official. Diligent, promising, and loyal to the State. At least, that’s what your superiors believe.

In truth, you work for the underground. You steal classified documents, sabotage operations, and help the resistance. But there’s something you’re hiding even from your comrades.

Welcome to the Ministry! Here, you’ll process citizens’ files, sign orders, and steadily climb the career ladder. But your real work begins when you leave your desk.

Every employee has their own routine, weaknesses, and secrets. And your assignments won’t lead you to all of them. Sometimes, you just need to be in the right place at the right time.

By day, you serve the State. In secret, you work for those who dream of destroying it.

The Ministry orders you to find a traitor among your colleagues. The underground asks you to help that same person escape. Your superior offers a promotion that will grant you access to classified archives. But your new position will require you to sign arrest orders yourself. Where will your loyalties lie?

Carry out assignments for both sides, gather intelligence, prepare underground operations, and decide whom to help. The State isn’t always wrong, the resistance isn’t always right, and your own interests may matter more than either cause.

Your workday is over. You return home with stolen documents—and suddenly, there’s a knock at the door. The police are here to search your apartment. You have seconds to hide the evidence of your double life.

With every search, the police become more persistent. One day, they may arrive knowing exactly what they’re looking for.

You’re used to looking inside other people’s closets. Now try to keep everyone out of yours.

Even in a world of total control, there’s room for love. But trusting someone here is more dangerous than it seems.

Meet four very different women. Get to know their personalities, help them with personal problems, flirt, go on dates, and develop romantic relationships. Some work for the State; others belong to the resistance. Each has her own beliefs, desires, and secrets.

But what happens if the woman you love ends up on the other side? Or asks you to do something that goes against your orders?

In Beholder IV, there’s no “do the right thing” button.

You can save someone from arrest—or sign the order that ruins their life. You can help the resistance carry out an operation or secretly hand its plans to the State.

Steal the document you need. Alter a patrol schedule. Warn someone of danger. Or simply do nothing.

The game will remember your actions. Your decisions affect characters’ fates, relationships, the course of operations, and how the story unfolds. On your next playthrough, things could turn out very differently.

A loyal revolutionary? A ruthless careerist? A double agent using both sides for personal gain? A resistance leader? Or perhaps an oligarch in the service of the State? Or someone willing to betray them all for the answer to a single question?

Uncover the truth in Beholder IV—a new chapter in the dark dystopian series where everyone is watching everyone else. And now, they’re watching you.

I impale myself with a sword to heal? I'm sold!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I don't often play platformers, but when I do you can bet that it'll be a bloody hack and slash with tons of gore and creepy monsters. It's a high I've been chasing ever since finishing Blasphemous 2, and while I've not managed to find something that can rival the same theistic terror it offers, the new demo for Ichorous delivers on the gore.

The premise of Ichorous is simple: you play as The Warlock, an agile fellow who is bound to the god of blood by contract to kill monsters and collect their bloody ichor. The map itself is a puzzle with an unknown layout and number of rooms that you can only piece together by searching through them, killing as many foes as possible while progressing through the map.

The demo only has a couple of levels so far, the Thrall Grave being the first and the Squalor being the second. Each one has different grunts, mini-bosses, and a final level boss for you to tear to shreds. There's giant putrid flying insects that spit phlegm at you, angry cages with several arms all swinging swords at you, and multi-headed bloodthirsty maggots that also have, you guessed it, swords..

The ichor you get from killing these beasts can be exchanged for offerings, upgrades that scale as you progress through each level. But with each offering comes a curse. It's a random modifier that can change bosses or even the map layout. For example, after killing the first level boss I chose Mob Tactics, which gives my character the ability to dart between foes, rapidly slashing at them, after I kill an enemy. The downside is, however, that rooms now have a 10% chance to not spawn brutes and instead spawn fiends and vermin twice. Meaning I'll have double the work and half the payout.

These offerings will also change and grow stronger as you do, giving you one more thing to worry about as you progress through a run. There are also small trinkets to be found around the map that act as minor upgrades, which can strengthen your chosen build. But like all roguelikes, once you die that's it. You're left to start again, collect new offerings, curses, and trinkets as you try to progress through the map once again.

It's not a hard reset though as some mini-bosses will disappear from the map once you've killed them. Leaving just the ones you haven't bested yet, and grunts roaming around each room. Some purists may not appreciate this, but I sure do. It's nice having some evidence of your hard work, especially when you've managed to get so far through a run.

But the biggest advantage you take away from each failed attempt, as usual, is what you've learned.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It took a couple of runs for me to get going, but once everything clicked I managed to figure out attack patterns, routes, and what the best build for me would be going forward; it's leeches by the way, always the ball of leeches.

The demo ended after I completed the first level by stabbing a big ball of organic tissue named The Clot repeatedly and bested the second level doing the same to a monster with a ball of spikes for a head. The fights were both challenging and fair, attacks were consistent so it just meant I had to take a couple of steps back at first and learn the movements. Neither took particularly long to take down, and honestly, I was really sad once it was all over.

Ichorous is still in its early stages but I'm really excited to see what more it'll bring to the table. It already seems to offer everything I want from action platformers: fun fights, disgusting enemies, loads of blood, a wide range of rewarding upgrades, and a fantastic soundtrack. Honestly, I was sold on Ichorous as soon as I realised that in order to heal myself I first had to absorb the blood of my enemies that had been spattered across the room and then stab myself through the chest with my blade. Hell yeah, more of that please.

#3853. County of Fortune, now out in early access, is a medieval city builder that asks, why limit yourself to just one city?

Don't count your towns before they've hatched

I know what you want. The humble city builder isn't enough for you any more, is it? You need a cities builder, you can't just stop at one, but you don't want to build up an entirely different city on a new save file. If it were up to you, they'd all be on the same map, a motorway's worth of a drive away from each other. If we're talking contemporary cities, I can't help you, but if you can settle for numerous medieval towns across an entire county, then County of Fortune should do just fine.

County of Fortune just landed in early access a couple of days ago, and as mentioned (and as the name suggests), you're building up an entire county! "You place whole settlements across the county and lay each one out on a medieval grid. Each one grows, specializes, and knits into a living region where rivers and resources decide what thrives," the game's Steam page explains. "As the county matures, a second game begins. Named mayors run each settlement. Rival noble houses weave politics across the region. And migrating cultures bless some villages, while complicating others."

To start with, it's up to you where you want to place each of your settlements, deciding how they individually function as you do. The towns are then partially procedurally generated as they get built up, slowly connecting to other nearby towns. "The scale is the point. You are not zooming into a single town - you are zooming out to see a whole county come to life." A big part of the strategy comes down to how you navigate the map; finding resource deposits, picking appropriate terrain profiles, utilising rivers efficiently, finding a good climate, setting good trade routes, it's all about working with the land you've got.

Each settlement will produce different things depending on the materials available to them in close proximity, meaning each one has a unique function. You've got different types of characters to consider too: mayors, noble houses and cultures, all intersecting with different elements of how a town functions. Seems like a unique approach to city building! And as mentioned, it's out in early access; you can pick it up on Steam here.

#3852. Nintendo game sales surge thanks to Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, but Switch 2 hardware suffers big decline

Nintendo's latest financial earnings report is here, revealing healthy software sales thanks to the enormously popular Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. Sales of Switch 2 hardware, however, are down.

As per Nintendo's 2nd Quarter fiscal earnings report, focusing on the three-month period ending 30th September 2026, Switch 2 hardware registered a big drop in sales during the first half of the current financial year (FY27).

Over that period, Nintendo sold 6.49m Switch 2 units and 1.27m units of the original Switch - equating to a 37.4 percent decline for Switch 2 and 32.7 percent decline for Switch 1 compared to the same period last year. Nintendo had previously forecast a decline in hardware sales, and the company still expects to sell 16.50m Switch 2 units by the end of the current fiscal year.

Nintendo software sales, on the other hand, saw a big year-on-year boost of 18.8 percent on Switch 2 (to 24.49m units) and a smaller increase of 6.8 percent on Switch 1. That's all thanks to the release of several popular first- and third-party titles over the first half of FY27. Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream was by far the most successful game with 8.81m units sold, followed by Rhythm Heaven Groove at 2.89m. Splatoon Raiders (the only Switch 2 exclusive of the three) sold 2.42m. Nintendo also highlighted a 60.5 percent year-on-year increase in digital game sales.

The increase in software unit sales and the "continued weakness of the Yen" couldn't prevent the overall business from declining by 15.3 percent year-on-year, however.

Other remaining releases in Nintendo' s current fiscal year include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (which launches today and was awarded five stars in Eurogamer's review), Switch 2 re-releases of Pikmin 2 and Xenoblade Chronicles 3, as well as Metroid Ravenous, which arrives early in 2027.

#3851. Mass Effect petition has enough signatures for the Canadian Government to potentially save BioWare

Following news of EA's decision to shut down iconic RPG studio BioWare, Canadian fans of the studio have escalated their grievances to the governmental level, calling on the Canadian Government to step in and save the Canadian studio from closure, seemingly after Canada's New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis called on the government to do so.

Fans have submitted a petition to the Canadian House of Commons arguing for the government to find a way for BioWare to continue, such as through funding that allows the studio to buy the Mass Effect and other IPs and go independent.

The petition, number e-7898, argues that "BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports" and that the studio's closure by its American parent company "represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," it continued.

The petition opened for signatures on 4th of November, and has already amassed 1,700 signatures. By law, petitions that surpass 500 valid signatures from Canadian citizens or residents are entered into the House of Commons' agenda, meaning they will be presented in front of the parliament.

As encouraging as that may be, it's worth keeping in mind that it may not result in meaningful change. Even if the Canadian Government agrees with the petition's goals, it cannot force EA to sell BioWare or its various IPs.

EA notably didn't shop the studio around before closing it down, and the publisher has a history of closing down owned studios rather than selling them off. EA has also kept the IPs of its various shuttered studios.

The community's reaction to BioWare's closure has taken different forms. Hundreds of thousands signed a different petition to save Mass Effect. The people behind the movement have purchased billboards in Times Square in New York City to advertise it, with plans for more outside The Game Awards ceremony in December.

Meanwhile, former BioWare developers have spoken about the last days of BioWare, and the work they've poured into Mass Effect Universe, the studio's final project before it was shuttered.

#3850. Echoes of Mirror's Edge, Dishonored and a dream set in Italy I once had can be found in Boars in Rome, an expressive parkour platformer set in dystopian Rome

Years ago, I had this dream where I was parkouring through a greatly sunken version of Venice, no doubt sourced from the many hours I put into Assassin's Creed 2 as a teen who should have been studying for their GCSEs a lot more than they were. It's stuck with me after all this time mostly because of how much I wanted to capture that feeling again somehow, as the real Assassin's Creed didn't quite cut it. And lo and behold, there I was today browsing Bluesky when I came across Boars in Rome, a Mirror's Edge and Counter Strike Surf inspired parkour platformer set in a dystopian version of Rome.

Truthfully, witnessing the clip I've shared below was baffling to me. "This is what I dreamt of!" More or less, anyway, for the setting isn't quite the same; "You have been selected to start a new life off planet. Earth has been abandoned," explains the game's Steam page. "Machines keep working and nature claims what remains. Find out what happened while you were frozen in time by exploring the remnants of Rome where historical monuments mix with futurist megastructures."

Mirrors Edge x Counter Strike Surf where you parkour on anything! Be smooth n stylish in dystopian Rome. Or just jump around and explore, whatever works for you. It's called Boars in Rome! #PitchYaGame[image or embed]

Not all of it matches that dream of mine, some of it leans much more into brutalism than the typical, much older architecture you'd expect of Rome, but it's there nonetheless. In motion, Boars in Rome feels quite oneiric too. There is so much more control over the game's avatar than what my real body is capable of, or wants to do. You can run, jump, slide and wallrun, positioning it quite closely to VHOLUME mechanically. Where it differs is in its additives, movement tech like being able to swing on lampposts or vault over low down obstacles.

VHOLUME is more of a game about providing you with a simple toolkit and leaving you to push it to its maximum. Boars in Roam is a touch more expressive, and I'd dare to even call it an immersive sim. The levels you can romp around are linear, you have an end point to reach, only the journey is up to you. It certainly feels appropriate to put it in the im sim camp given that, at least the game's first level, calls to mind Viktor Antonov's work on Dishonored (and Half-Life 2, too, honestly).

As it currently stands, there's no release date for Boars in Rome, but there is a playtest you can sign up and gain immediate access to if you fancy a go yourself; you can do so on Steam right here, or at least pop it a wishlist.

Against my better judgement, I've been getting into MOBAs a little bit this year. Unfortunately, mucking around in League of Legends' ARAM with my veteran pals felt like a hydrogen bomb (them, the videogame) versus a coughing baby (me playing any champ that wasn't Yuumi).

Welcome to Critical Hit, where I (or someone else on the PC Gamer team) celebrate and lament all things videogame music, audio design, and the ways our favourite games make our ears tingle.

So when they all decided to get into Deadlock a few weeks ago, I took it as an opportunity to dive in alongside them—partly thanks to being utterly inundated with Rem-related posts from one of my close pals in the days prior. And you know what? It's good. I'm admittedly a bit of a MOBA disliker—from the outside looking in, it's an awful lot of faff and jargon and a high skill ceiling that I'm not traditionally ready to work towards.

But where Deadlock is concerned? I might just put that effort in. It's not just because of its gameplay (which is very good, mind) but the fact that Valve has created one of the coolest, vibe-iest games I've played in a hot sec. It looks great, it feels great, and most importantly for this here column that you're reading, it sounds amazing.

From the very first moments of the main menu's playfully ominous jazz notes, I was sold. It perfectly encapsulates this strange, eerie 1950s New York that's all about performing rituals and summoning elder gods.

If Valve knows how to do anything with its music in Deadlock, it's how to perfectly build this sense of anticipation and foreboding. The track that plays when you're in the Hideout—Deadlock's lobby, essentially—is subtle. Almost so subtle that you might not notice it over the chaos of your pals spamming ultimates off cooldown in the adjacent training room. But it sports this mysterious finesse befitting of a supernatural gang preparing to unleash havoc across New York.

That tension builds even further when you get into the character select screen, which dials up the creepiness just that touch more. And then, finally, searching for a match layers even more instruments on top with this delightful little drum beat that dances between each ear. Having the track slowly unfurl the way it does across the process of loading in and searching for a match? It's honestly bloody brilliant.

For me, though, two tracks stand out above all others: For the King, and Street Brawl's item draft jingle.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

For the King is a mere 41 seconds(!!) long, used when you're placed on the Hidden King team for your match. It's got this gnarly riff that almost sounds like it's being blasted through the broken speakers of your high school sweetheart's secondhand car, but it's good. It's the perfectly evil vibe, and has me secretly wishing I'll get Hidden King over Archmother every time I load into a game.

And it is such a shame that I do not mesh with Street Brawl, because the music that plays while you're picking your items between rounds? Hoo boy. I cannot overstate how clever it feels as a track. It once again digs deep for that sense of mystery—fitting, considering all of your items are random—but the entire time, in the background, you can hear the ticking of a clock. It permeates through the rest of the track at random intervals, but it's always there.

That ticking feels like such a brilliant little detail, considering you only get a short amount of time to flip through each item set and pick the ones you want to add to your arsenal. Take too long to pick? The music switches up, becoming more urgent and almost uncomfortable to listen to as the clock ticks down to the round beginning.

I know I shouldn't have underestimated Valve considering all of the very good music it has made over the years, but I wasn't expecting to be so thoroughly impressed with Deadlock's soundtrack as I am. It's some of the most thoughtful, exciting, charismatic composing I've had the pleasure of listening to in years, and the fact that it actually makes me want to play a MOBA even more? That's just good song crafting.

#3848. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for waking up covered in sand. The roof of your house is missing. A small man stands in the emptied bed of a dump truck. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he says. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he repeats. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he declares once again, beginning to move towards you this time. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6." You realise your hands are tied down. Oh no.

Is he about to sit on your face? WAIT, THAT'S NOW ILLEGAL HERE IN THE UK. NO, PLEASE, DON'T SIT ON MY-time seems to slow as the bare backside approaches your visage. As its cheeks prepare to become as sandy as yours, you hear its wielder say: "And we thought, hey, given the moment..."

Panicking, you scrabble for anything to say which might free you before something that might get a British MP's hackles up can occur. "Things first went awry when I turned up for my appointment to find a tall German man wearing a cowboy hat asking a PR if he could play the game," you blurt out. The posterior momentarily stops moving towards you. Buoyed, you continue to tell a story you heard from VGC's Chris Scullion.

I was asked if I minded sharing my one-to-one appointment with this chap too, to which my inherent British cowardly courtesy kicked in and I lied that it was perfectly fine.

"I want drums", he said as he entered the room. "We are playing Dani California by Red Hot Chili Peppers." Rather than ask him whether he also fancied telling me where I was going for dinner later, I picked up my guitar and went along with it, eager to just play the game.

The bottom begins its agonising crawl towards your kisser once more. You can feel the occupants of parliamentary benches begin to sense a disturbance in the force. Maybe if you can make the bumholder sad, that'll do the trick. You try to remember how Sebastian Cardoso of Game Studio Unlocked's presentation on the tragic fates of game studios after acquisitions went.

A hundred and twenty-three of the 362 developers were shut outright. The average life from acquisition to closure is 6.4 years and the median is 5, meaning half of all closed studios were dead within five years of their acquisition.

The familiar names mostly died fast. EA closed Pandemic two years after buying it. Sony shut Firewalk barely a year and a half in. Warner Bros. closed Player First roughly seven months after acquiring it. Bluepoint, closed at the five-year mark, is exactly what the median looks like.

It's no use. That arse's shadow its creeping across ever more of your face like your're a planet with a nose and it's the Vogon Constructor Fleet. Maybe you can somehow contort your head to the side. Arrrggghh. You call on all the strength of muscles you barely ever use and think of the incredible gymnastic feats executed by Physical Contortion Gamer's Josh Wolens during an ongoing GTA diary series.

Attempting to do flips, then, just sort of rotates your entire body below the diaphragm while your head and chest area remain bolt upright, rigid in such a way that you could feasibly fly a flag from your own thorax.

Which looks odd. Nevertheless, it is pretty fun to scoot and roll your way through Los Santos. At one point, I attempted a double frontflip in the middle of a part of the map that had been deleted for some reason. It didn't quite work out, and I ended up colliding with and possibly killing a man in a fursuit.

It doesn't work. You can't get away. You begin to scream. The posterioperator stops repeating the words "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6". Instead, he asks where that mysterious German cowboy you mentioned earlier has gone. You don't have a clue, and can't help admitting as much. "Ah well." The derriere resumes its descent, now mere inches from your mug. This is the end. You have one last rummage through your mind for possible solutions.

Respec's Tom Orry hasn't managed to save you. "Fine, sit on my face and send me to hell," you shout into the pinkish ring of doom as British cops prepare to ram-raid your abode and arrest you for crimes against a prude's definition of acceptable shagging.

The bum stops. Its owner asks if you've just said the word Sentinel. "Yes," you lie.

The arse is raised and swapped for the face of a man. "What a perfect time for you to realise what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called," he says.

You notice he's not Todd Howard. Or Adrian Edmondson.

"It's Ade's month off and they needed another baldy to play this esteemed role," Sir Patrick Stewart announces, clearly responding the look of befuddlement your face can still have since it hasn't been crushed by a ten-tonne tush. You wonder how you didn't recognise his voice before, especially given he played the emperor in Oblivion.

"Here's to the next Bethesda game after Starfield," the Stew sings as the police bust through the door and he's beamed up before they can tackle him.

#3847. World of Warcraft: Forever's seemingly stellar launch continues as it soars to the top of Twitch's most viewed games, beating out the likes of League of Legends and Zelda

World of Warcraft: Forever launched last night after a hugely successful beta, and it's not just players getting in on the fun. Blizzard's MMO is also proving quite the attraction for spectators, soaring all the way up to the top of Twitch's most viewed games.

As of writing, World of Warcraft sits at around 385,000 viewers and streamer Ahmpy has the most popular WoW channel, pulling in around 18,300 live viewers.

For comparison, Twitch's ever-popular non-gaming Just Chatting category is the service's second most watched category with 145,000 viewers, and Riot Games' genre-leading MOBA League of Legends takes third place with 81,400 viewers.

Aion 2, another MMO released back in October, is sitting pretty at around 75,900 viewers, while Nintendo's newly released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (it's good!) has brought in a wonderful 63,100 watchers on the day of its arrival.

Perhaps contributing to World of Warcraft: Forever's success is the fact it launched with few problems, enjoying one of the smoothest day-one releases in the series' recent history. Its beta proved especially popular, with Blizzard developers calling it one of the most successful betas they've ever seen. One wonders how many of these current Twitch viewers are adults getting their WoW fix during work while their boss isn't looking?

James Gunn says "the characters we set up will live on" as he departs as the co-CEO of DC Studios

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

James Gunn has released a separate, lengthy statement amid the news that he and co-CEO Peter Safran are no longer the heads of DC Studios.

"There have been so many highs along the way: releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs., the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments," Gunn wrote on his personal Instagram account.

Gunn also lamented that he "disliked the at-times corporate nature of the job" and had the "most difficulty" with "dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

"So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I'm also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That's not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we've just been engaged on another DC project which I'm writing, and we'll see where it goes after that. And of course, the characters we set up will live on." You can read the full statement below.

The statement comes amid the shocking news that Gunn and Safran would be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham, effective December 1. The duo was first appointed to the position back in 2022, having released three movies: Superman, Supergirl, and Clayface, and four TV shows: Creature Commandos, Peacemaker season 2, The Penguin, and Lanterns, over the last four years. Still to come are Man of Tomorrow, The People V Gorilla Grodd, Creature Commandos season 2, and the long-awaited The Batman: Part II.

Of course, this change is no doubt part of the Skydance merger, which sees Paramount in full control of Warner Bros. and everything Warner Bros. owns. It's worth noting that, before Gunn and Safran were appointed, Warner Bros. executives reportedly wanted an overhaul of DC in favor of putting classic heroes back at the forefront and making them a bit less dark/more kid-friendly. That said, it's possible that Skydance executives want fewer projects like The People v. Gorilla Grodd and Creature Commandos, and more big-hitters on screen, like Wonder Woman or Aquaman... and finally Batman (who still only exists as part of Matt Reeves' Elseworlds; the DCU has yet to cast a Batman). It also probably doesn't help that Supergirl was a massive critical and commercial failure.

Man of Tomorrow hits theaters on July 9, 2027. For more, here are all the upcoming DC movies and shows announced before Gunn's departure.

#3845. Uh oh, Zelda fans have accidentally created a mix between kid and adult Link, and the result is hilarious

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time‘s remake is out, seemingly capturing the magic of the original and possibly even more. Fans have stumbled upon a puzzling new version of Link the developers definitely didn’t have in mind. Time to meet the new member of the Zelda family.

In the original Ocarina of Time, Link only ever gets the silver gauntlets chest as a child. In the remake, he’s only supposed to get it as a child as well, but he can actually get them as Adult Link via a glitch that triggers a very unique time paradox-like reaction.

Since Link’s only ever supposed to get these as an adult, getting them earlier on will cause the game to fit the adult Link’s model into the tiny one, a desperate move that will seriously impact his looks.

Using a glitch to get a really big jump in the remake, its now possible to get the silver gauntlets chest as adult, which is supposed to be gotten as child. The cutscene that plays after tries to fit adult link into child link model, which ends up looking like this. pic.twitter.com/un9DflnvxT

Some are calling this new creature “Child Adult Link,” others named him “Lunk.” but everyone is cherishing his miraculous birth, regardless of how unintentional it might’ve been.

Better yet, Lunk is seemingly not even the only new somewhat Link-shaped lifeform in the game. Some other fans have shared it’s also possible to create a reverse form of Lunk, which creates, ugh… Adult Child Link? Lank? I don’t know what to call it, and I don’t even know how you get to morph your Link into this other version. What I can definitely tell you is what you’ll be thinking as soon as you lay your eyes on it, which is that it also looks hilarious.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

And look, puberty is a strange phase for everyone. It’s actually completely normal that either “new” version of Link looks pretty awkward. There’s a reason why the original timeskips from kid Link into his adult version. Still, this accidental addition makes the remake even more nostalgic, as it can now remind the many of us who enjoyed the original during our strangest times that things would eventually turn out fine.

And, even if that’s not enough, there are even some fans who are liking “Lunk” for what he is, pointing out his resemblance to a very popular Internet figure.

Though Nintendo’s take on the remake’s aesthetic left the fan base considerably divided, this is exactly the kind of thing that the whole community will enjoy and possibly even elevate into an all-time meme—something all 10/10 games deserve.

You can now play the Zelda Ocarina of Time remake on the Nintendo Switch 2.

#3844. Ahead of The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past, here's a "lore friendly unofficial expansion to Geralt's life in Toussaint" from a well-established quest modder

While its remastered upgrade might have broken cover in late September, The Witcher 3's extra expansion isn't set to join it until next year. With 2027 still a month and a bit away, a modder's taken it upon themselves to add a few more adventures to Geralt's time in Toussaint, Blood and Wine's gorgeous French-ish duchy, before the bloke from the river heads off to Letten for Songs of the Past.

So far, only the opening chapter of the mod - Annals of the Duchy - has been released. It adds in a new quest about Geralt, with help from either Yen or Triss if either have made the trip out to Toussaint as part of your playthrough, getting into a scrape thanks to a halfling who seems to promise Gerry the chance to juice up his vineyard's vines.

The mod's creator, Jontej, has previously put together a couple of other custom Witcher 3 quests. While they do look to have used AI voices in English versions of those mods, for Annals of the Duchy they've enlisted a cast of human actors for both Enlish and Polish versions.

Jontej has plans to expand this new questline going forwards, having cited specific "plans for an extra storyline involving Syanna", whom you might remember from Blood and Wine's main quest. Given that - spoilers ahead - the mod relies on you having gotten the Blood and Wine ending which sees both Anna Henrietta and Syanna survive, as well as having paid to renovate the gardens of Geralt's vineyard. They add that, when it comes to their additions, the "timeline fits quite well [with] the upcoming official Songs of the Past Expansion, which has been confirmed to take place after the events of the main game/Blood and Wine".

As much as I've argued that, as of right now, I struggle to see how Songs of the Past will manage to outdo Blood and Wine as a satisfying end to Geralt's tale in the Witcher game trilogy, I am intrigued by the idea of a few more modded adventures showing Gerry adjusting to the semi-retired life. After all, Toussaint's got to have a few more dungeons tucked away that're worth temporarily dusting off the White Wolf's twin swords for.

To kick off Annals of the Duchy, you'll need to trigger its first quest by taking a stroll from the Corvo Bianco manor house down to its gardens between 11am and 1pm. It's worth noting that any other mod which messes with Yen, Triss or companions in general has a chance to muck things up as far as Jontej's creation goes.

#3843. Nintendo says it isn't planning any more Switch 2 price hikes

Nintendo, which unveiled the results of the first half of its fiscal year 2027 earlier today, has now said it has access to enough quantities of memory to manufacture more Switch 2 consoles.

As a result, the platform holder does not plan to increase the price of the Switch 2. That's according to Reuters, citing Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa.

Nintendo, which has so far sold 26m Switch 2 consoles, has already raised the price of the console earlier this year. The price hikes, which took effect on 1st September in the US, Canada, Japan and Europe, saw the console's price increase by $50 / €30 / ¥10,000. Although that was technically the first price hike for the console itself, prior to the Switch 2's launch last year, Nintendo raised the price of Switch 2 accessories in the US as a result of the Trump Administration's tariffs.

The reason that would cause Nintendo to raise prices again is the same that already caused rival PlayStation and Xbox to do so: AI-driven, global memory and storage shortages.

PlayStation already raised PS5 and PS5 Pro prices, on several occasions. Xbox has likewise gone through multiple rounds of price hikes for its Series X and Series S consoles, with the most recent having taken place in August.

That same crisis pushed one of Nintendo's longtime ROM suppliers to exit the business, opting instead to focus on the more lucrative business segments. ROM memory is used in Switch cartridges, though Nintendo hasn't commented on the news.

Incidentally, Switch 2 hardware sales have been in decline for several quarters now compared to its banner launch in 2025. Still, Switch 2 sales are tracking ahead of the Switch 1.

Speaking on a new episode of The Examined Game, Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith shared his big takeaway from Baldur's Gate 3, and contrasted the approaches Bethesda and Larian have taken in their respective RPGs.

"The surprises come with the little things, not the big things. I have a long history with D&D as well as Bethesda. For me, it was joyful to see the D&D expression of fantasy rules come to life. Larian Studios did a magnificent job of that. I also thought that they redefined things in a certain way. Bethesda games have always had the philosophy of, let the player play everything.

"You can play the entire Thieves' Guild, you can play the entire Fighters' Guild, you can play the entire Mages' Guild, etc. There is nothing that your character can't play. That's a very good philosophy. I support that philosophy. But I was pleasantly surprised to see how positive it felt to me to make consequential decisions that closed off gameplay in Baldur's Gate.

"That also felt good, because it was done well. I felt like the decisions I made had more meaning in certain ways, because there were actual consequences. If I wanted to see those other [outcomes], I'd have to bring up another character and try different paths.

"They were both fun, they're just fun in different ways, and that, to me, was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things [where] you couldn't have both. The lesson learned is: You can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way, and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

I think Nesmith is 100% correct, and it's really Bethesda's lane to offer relatively unhindered fantasy fulfillment in its games. You generally see players and modders be the ones to introduce roleplaying-oriented restrictions, while Bethesda maximizes freedom.

At the same time, I've always thought that what separates Bethesda games from more pure sim sandboxes like Mount & Blade is that the studio provides the player with just enough structure and narrative to push back on. I think there's room to experiment there, and examples in Bethesda's own back catalogue of where it can take things.

Morrowind springs to mind: The Fighters' and Thieves' Guilds are opposed to each other, and their quests are mutually exclusive after a point⁠—you even directly sabotage the other guild in each questline. The Mages' Guild and House Telvanni are similarly opposed, and the Dunmer Houses pretty much all hate each other.

But you don't even have to go all the way back to 2002: Skyrim has three major examples in the Civil War questline, the Dawnguard expansion, and the alternate ending to the Dark Brotherhood story. Siding with the Penitus Oculatus in "Destroy the Dark Brotherhood" isn't as substantial as the faction quest you're throwing away, but it is a very cool addition that enhances Skyrim's sense of depth and stakes. I'd love to see more like it in TES6: Sentinel⁠—wouldn't it be rad to have a full questline for both the secret police and the assassins' guild?

I caught on Nesmith's choice of words that he enjoyed Baldur's Gate 3's approach "because it was done well." I've certainly encountered content-blocking choices in games that felt cheap or forced. I'm a huge CD Projekt fan, but I'll always be a hater when it comes to The Witcher 2's mutually exclusive second acts. I think the same idea was executed much better in Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty.
