#3841. Extraction shooters need a PvE mode for casual players—so what’s the controversy?

This idea isn't half as controversial as half of you make it out to be.

Any major extraction shooter release inevitably summons the age-old debate of PvE vs. PvP. It’s been the case with ARC Raiders and DMZ, and that schism will resurface whenever the next one launches. You can always count on heated arguments stirring controversy about something that shouldn’t be controversial at all.

After all, how dare players enjoy PvE in a PvPvE game? The way the debate often goes, you’d assume it was a cardinal sin, like the PvE crowd was planning to personally tar and feather every PvP player in existence.

Instead, PvE players often just want a more forgiving, relaxed experience that does not involve getting ratted to death in Stella Montis or having to spend an entire match in Hajin with one’s butthole clenched so tightly that not even a Wi-Fi signal passes through it. And from the looks of it, this isn’t a small crowd, either.

Take ARC Raiders, for example. The demand for a PvE mode was so large that Embark tested a toggle that disabled damage between players last month. Before then, 37 percent of its fanbase (and growing) were focused on PvE cooperation, 34 were there purely for PvP (stable since launch), and 27 landed in the middle, Embark said. Over 51 percent of all surveyed users showed interest in a dedicated PvE mode, according to the studio.

If even the thought of discussing this makes you feel like Ben Affleck with a cigarette, you’re not the only one who’s exhausted. The PvE vs. PvP argument is the reheated leftovers from the skill-based matchmaking debate, annoyingly inescapable when battle royales were all the rage.

Often, the higher-skill players don’t want to match against others of similar ability because their games get too difficult and stop being fun. And yes, this is exactly what happens to lower-skill players without SBMM.

Activision ran a famous experiment with its matchmaking in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 in 2024. The company loosened the skill constraints for half of its players during a month. At the end of the test, it noted that the 10 percent of affected players at the top of the skill pyramid returned more often, but the remaining 90 percent were considerably less likely to come back. And that’s with a diluted SBMM.

“If [SBMM] were completely removed, we would expect to see the player population erode rapidly in the span of a few months, resulting in a negative outcome for all our players,” the study said.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

PvP is zero-sum by definition: for one to win, another must lose. Unsurprisingly, it doesn’t feel good to be on the losing side. Having the chance to opt out of that and into a different playstyle altogether shouldn’t cause this much uproar—especially not in a game where keeping gear plays a major role. And often, it doesn’t even relate exclusively to skill, but the type of experience one wants to have.

This time, it’s not even a matter of catering to one part of the audience in detriment of another, which would be an understandable concern if it made a modicum of sense. Embark isn’t going to make your fingers fall off every time you shoot another player. Having PvE in DMZ won’t make Activision cease content for Warzone or multiplayer, otherwise CoD Zombies wouldn’t exist.

Often, the people contemplated by PvE mode aren’t even in the game, but they’re yearning to be. The lack of full-on PvE in DMZ didn’t make me flock to multiplayer; it made me uninstall the game altogether. I only bought ARC Raiders because of the PvE test and the game’s aggression-based matchmaking. If that went away, I’d disappear with it. My friends did so the second the PvE test ended, and they’re eagerly waiting for the mode to return.

Extraction shooters being unapproachable made sense when they were niche. Now that every live-service seems to flirt with the genre, though, they should be more welcoming, especially if they want to draw a larger crowd.

As an avid frequenter of friendly lobbies in ARC Raiders, I’ve had more positive experiences with randoms than I can count, and that’s a big reason why I open the game. I’m having one hell of a time fighting Matriarchs, defibbing other raiders, and dropping duplicate blueprints. My archenemy was a cat bed, and I’m thrilled this was the case. It sucks when it’s tooth-and-nail all the time, as every big opponent of SBMM will tell you.

The difference is, unlike hero shooters or battle royales, extraction shooters already have a PvE element baked into them, no retrofitting required. Of course, you may have to reshuffle some things, like increasing the difficulty of the AI-controlled enemies to raise the threat and keep players on their toes. But it’s different from creating something entirely new, like if people wanted bots in Apex Legends or full-blooded PvP in the extraction-adjacent Helldivers 2. And it’s certainly not too much to ask.

There’s a reason extraction shooters were somewhat obscure before the gaming industry threw a borderline infinite amount of money at making the genre mainstream. Soulslikes aside, not everyone wants to get their teeth kicked in as a pastime. Sure, the cutthroat uncertainty from PvPvE shaped the identity of ARC Raiders, but there are ways to evoke that without fighting other players, as Helldivers 2 and GTFO have proved.

ARC Raiders has come a long way in the past year, in no small part because of the 37 percent of PvE players (and in bigger part because of the 63 percent of other raiders). Maybe the burgeoning PvE scene changes the vision of the game somewhat, and that’s fine. DMZ getting a fully PvE mode wouldn’t be entirely out of the realm of possibility, considering that’s basically what MWZ was. That’s the beauty and bane of live services: there’s always room for reinvention.

#3840. Rockstar were "definitely" thinking about giving a Japanese studio the keys to GTA, says former tech director - "I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it"

Obbe Vermeij on ancient plans for a GTA Tokyo

Since time immemorial, North American and European publishers have racked their brains over ways to make their games sell in Japan, ancient heartland of mythical beings like Mario, Sonic, and Polaroid Pete. In the late noughties, Microsoft launched a big push to give Japanese youth the Xbox virus with such targeted console exclusives as Blue Dragon and Lost Odyssey. And Rockstar once dreamed of making a Grand Theft Auto game set in Tokyo.

Speaking to me last week, Rockstar North's former technical director Obbe Vermeij shared a little about the abandoned project. Emphasis on the "little" – it doesn't appear to have gotten very far, despite recently unearthed allusions to "Tokyo PS2" in GTA 5's source code.

Rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive filed a trademark for GTA Tokyo back in 2003, the year before the release of the Los Angeles-flavoured GTA: San Andreas. At the time, Rockstar were apparently looking at collaborating with a Japanese studio on the project. "So this was kind above my pay grade," Vermeij told me. "But yeah, there were negotiations with studios, and I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it, because then it becomes like a bigger thing than it is, and I'll probably get it wrong, and I don't know how far the negotiations were, how serious it was. I mean, it was definitely serious. It was the plan. But I don't know how close it got to actually happening."

The game itself would likely have been a contemporary story, not a historical yarn like Rockstar's subsequent Red Dead Redemption. "It definitely had samurai swords in it, I remember that, but I think it was present-day probably," Vermeij went on. "Or sort of not too [far off] - it wasn't, like, sort of the medieval era in Japanese history, or anything. It was definitely not like that."

Vermeij was at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009, where he worked on the first four mainline 3D GTA games, plus some handheld spin-offs. During that time, he says, Rockstar frequently considered the idea of a Grand Theft Auto set outside the United States. "In the same way that we were always thinking about other games, we also thought about cities that would be cool, and it was always the same list," he said. "It was Moscow, London. Istanbul, Rio de Janeiro, maybe Paris and Tokyo. It was always the same ones that people suggested."

Grand Theft Auto has never quite the money-spinner in Japan that it is in North America and Europe. Localised editions of the original three 3D GTA games were published by Capcom, sometime after the original releases, selling a few hundred thousand copies apiece in their launch years.

"I think perhaps [Rockstar's co-founders] the Housers were a little annoyed that GTA wasn't as big in Japan as they thought it deserved to be," Vermeij reflected. "So it kind of made sense to get a local studio to do it. Japanese people actually kind of like different games from westerners a fair bit. For instance, they don't like first person shooters and stuff. So, it made sense to have a Japanese studio have a shot at it, and I think it would have been really cool, because you know, a GTA made by somebody else in Japanese culture – that's something I would probably play."

Take-Two ultimately abandoned their original "GTA Tokyo" trademark in 2008. It's not clear how much Rockstar have considered setting GTA overseas since Vermeij's day, but co-founder Dan Houser (who left the company in 2020) recently told podcaster Lex Fridman that they ultimately decided it wasn't a credible objective.

“We made a little thing in London 26 years ago - GTA London - for the top-down for PS1," he said. "That was pretty cute and fun, as the first mission pack ever for PlayStation 1. I think for a full GTA game, we always decided there was so much Americana inherent in the IP, it would be really hard to make it work in London or anywhere else. You know, you needed guns, you needed these larger-than-life characters. It just felt like the game was so much about America, possibly from an outsider's perspective. But that was so much about what the thing was that it wouldn't really have worked in the same way elsewhere.”

If this article has left you pining for the Shibuya Scramble NPC-tipping sim that will never be, I bring good news: Japanese developers are quite capable of making their own urban open worlders. The obvious go-tos are Sega's Yakuza/Like A Dragon games, with their abundance of lovingly modelled eateries and discount stores. There's also Ghostwire: Tokyo, a respectable first-person parkour sim, though this particular incarnation of Tokyo has a lot of paranormal congestion. All these games have the advantage of being playable on PC right now. As for GTA 6? Who can say, but Vermeij thinks Rockstar might want to port it sooner to get ahead of the slopcomp craze.

#3838. How to get the Gold Lil’ Uzi Vert skin in Fortnite

The second week of Fortnite Treasure Hunters is all about Lil’ Uzi Vert, and you can get his Gold skin to add to your collection. However, this will be easier said than done once you explore the core method.

Let’s find out how to get this character skin added to your Treasure Hunters rewards.

The Lil’ Uzi Vert skin isn’t part of any pass, if you’re wondering. Instead, you can get it for free by simply opening the chests on your runs. Chests now have a different look, matching the spirits of the season.

The Lil’ Uzi Vert skin is part of the several items that are in the pool of rewards for week 2. These rewards, including the skin itself, will remain in the pool until the next Sunday, Nov. 15. While some rewards, like the Pirate Shop access token, will continue in the pool of rewards, the same can’t be said about the Lil’ Uzi Vert skin.

Hence, you’ll want to open as many chests as possible. Playing in squads also helps since you can open more chests together. Everyone gets the skin if one member manages to get the skin as a loot drop.

You can also target the different vaults that are located around the map. Opening them will reward you with Rare Chests that have better drop rates for rarer items.

Thanks to Epic Games, we now have a fair idea about the exact drop rate of this golden skin. Under ordinary conditions, you’ll have a 1:1562500 chance of obtaining the gold skin from a regular chest.

This makes it rarer than the Pirate Shop access token, which is remarkable to say the least. Power Hours will improve the odds in your favor, but it’s fair to say that the skin isn’t going to be dropping around like eggs.

If you find it, consider yourself to be extremely lucky. Otherwise, the next Power Hours on Nov. 14 will be your best shot when the odds will be boosted by 7.5x.

#3837. "There is no excuse for what I did," Nvidia CEO says, as affair with an alleged Chinese spy makes the US-China AI race look even more ridiculous

Just saying, Jensen, this probably doesn't happen if you stick to gaming GPUs

Ostensible graphics card company and definite AI giants Nvidia have commissioned an independent investigation into themselves, amid reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Per both the New York Times and Nvidia themselves, Nvidia offered to go under the microscope after US intelligence organisations elected to investigate Huang’s paramour, Chinese national Alice Huang (no, uh, relation, and also known as Huang Le), on suspicion of sharing sensitive information with Beijing. The Nvidia-running, leather-jacketed Huang has thus far only copped to an unspecified affair, admitting in an extraordinary public statement that he was "unfaithful to my wife." Still, the two investigations are likely to start a bizarre new leg in the alread-messy AI arms race that the US and China have been indulging in for years.

See, the basis for Huang and Huang’s relationship appears to be the same thing that’s been fucking us as PC owners: data centres and AI hardware. Alice Huang is a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who’ve bought billions of US dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips – and have been investigated for allegedly getting some of them into the hands of Chinese companies, in defiance of US trade restrictions on goods that might threaten the States’ AI dominance. Possibly also, given both countries’ increasing interest in the technology’s military uses, their perception of national security.

Many of these embargo-dodging accusations originate from after Alice Huang left Megaspeed, though she is now under that separate investigation for intelligence-sharing, and the prospect of any high-tech pillow talk from the lips of someone like Jensen Huang would be very disturbing to the feds indeed. Both Nvidia and their "deeply sorry" CEO deny that he shared sensitive information beyond that required for routine customer/client discussions.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the company’s statement reads. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

In the US-Sino battle of artificial intelligence, Jensen Huang has – as with his marriage – played both sides. He’s undoubtedly been a, perhaps the driving force behind reinventing Nvidia from beloved makers of gaming gear to the US’ number-one purveyors of environment-ruining, brain-polluting slop technology. But after the Biden administration banned American-made GPU exports to China over fears they’d be used to boost the latter’s military capabilities, Huang successfully lobbied Donald Trump into relaxing those restrictions, allowing Nvidia to flog their wares – including their crème de la crème AI GPU, the H200 – to cash-rich Chinese companies.

In a further twist, many of those chips have got mysteriously stuck in Hong Kong import facilities, suggesting the Chinese government in fact wants AI companies to stick to Chinese-made parts. But then, the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek reportedly trained their latest AI model on illicitly-gained Nvidia tech, so there’s either a healthy black market in operation, or the CCP is willing to tolerate the occasional bit of decadent Western silicone if it helps them catch up to the burger-chomping likes of ChatGPT and Claude. Maybe both, and either way, one can see how a well-placed honeypot could prove useful. Allegedly.

Without wanting to pick sides, in a race where I hope both teams lose, it’s also China who have more work to do. The People’s Republic produces a greater proportion of successful 'open' AI models, where the inner workings and even source code is made public, and mines more of the crucial minerals needed to build components and infrastructure. However, US-produced 'closed' models dominate global AI usage, and despite the lack of minerals, its existing data centres are estimated to wield 40 times the combined compute power of China’s. Probably because they just get all the RAM they need from Best Buy instead of digging it up themselves.

#3836. Remakes and new games "both have a place in the stable" says Nintendo boss, buoyed by the success of Star Fox and Ocarina of Time

It's been a good year for Nintendo: between Star Fox - the N64 classic with a dazzling facelift on Switch 2 - and the newly-launched and utterly fantastic Ocarina of Time remake, the platform holder is having a good run. And that's before you get to the likes of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, Mario Tennis Fever or any of the Switch 2 re-releases of first-party Switch games, like Xenoblade Chronicles 3 or Animal Crossing: New Horizons.

As popular as its other games are, though, you have to admit that 2026 has been a banner year for Nintendo's remakes - both Star Fox and Ocarina of Time have commanded plenty of headline-grabbing attention over the past 12 months, and it's a fact that isn't lost on the company. In a new interview with Polygon, Nintendo's Nate Bihldorff - senior vice president of product development and publishing - says that wholly new games and remakes of classics are of "equal importance" to the publisher going forward.

"I do think that new games and remakes both have a place in the Nintendo stable, of equal importance to be honest," Bihldorff told the site at the Ocarina of Time's launch event in New York City. "There are fans of every single IP that we have out there. Of course, having new games in those series is wonderful, and I look forward to them as much as anyone else does, but there’s also a deep satisfaction in revisiting games that were very, very special, like Ocarina of Time… But it's also important to think about how many people had never played the original, and for them, the remake of Ocarina of Time is going to be an absolutely brand-new, 2026 experience, and one that I just cannot wait for them to get their hands on."

There's more interesting stuff in the interview, as Bihldorff outlines his views on the strenght of the Nintendo roster - "it doesn't matter how excited I am about Donkey Kong Bananza at launch; there's always going to be more games that are coming down the pipeline" - and that the release pipeline continues to look as strong for the Switch 2 as it did for the Switch. "There's one constant that has been consistent through my entire career at Nintendo, and that's that you can pretty much set your watch by the idea that we're going to be coming out with stuff," Bihldorff told Polygon.

Ocarina of Time is off to a very strong start; aside from being critically adored, the game has taken off virally - I can't move on my own feeds for clips of the game, people reminiscing about their original memories of certain locations, or long posts about the nostalgic elements of the title. Star Fox, meanwhile, has 1.17 million copies worldwide since its launch earlier this year on the Nintendo Switch 2, making it the ninth best-selling game on the platform (this is via Nintendo's financials yesterday). I expect Ocarina will outpace that.

Whatever your personal opinon on remakes in games, you cannot deny that it is a large part of the industry - and it seems Nintendo is keen to ride that wave as far as it'll go.

With all that said, when will I get my Pokemon Black and White remakes, then?

As reported by Axios, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to carrying on an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean cloud computing company, Megaspeed. According to The New York Times, the Trump administration suspects Ms. Huang of passing information to China's Ministry of State Security. The Chinese government denies the accusation.

Both the NYT and Financial Times' previous reporting on Jensen Huang pursuing a romantic relationship with Alice Huang were contested by Nvidia, which had maintained that any relationship between the two was strictly professional.

Axios obtained a draft version of Jensen Huang's email apology to Nvidia employees. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang allegedly wrote. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did." Huang reportedly took "full responsibility" for the affair, but will not step down as Nvidia's CEO: "I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence."

Nvidia's board is organizing an independent committee to investigate the relationship, but does not believe company or national security secrets were compromised. Nvidia's board is not seeking Huang's removal from the CEO position.

This all comes as the US takes an increasingly hawkish stance toward China, framing AI development as a national security issue and restricting the sale of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. Meanwhile, US-based AI companies and their aggressive datacenter buildouts are proving increasingly unpopular with American voters.

I think I speak for all of us when I say: Damn, that's crazy. Remember when Jensen Huang was just the gaming graphics guy and not the AI apocalypse national security guy? Perhaps we were all happier in those simpler times, including Huang, whatever his skyrocketing net worth might say to the contrary.

It's only been a couple of months that we've known about the existence of Diablo 5, and as such there are a ton of open questions about the direction it'll take. Blizzard teased a few fundamentals during BlizzCon 2026, like the fact that it'll take place in a Sanctuary that's been completely overtaken by Diablo and his minions, and that there will no longer be any traditional towns or safe havens to hide from the bad guys. It's been clear to me that Blizzard is doubling down on the horror-driven bleakness that defined the first game in the series, and there are blatant call-backs to the series' roots in the itemization and procedurally generated environments, but there's still a lot left unanswered about what it'll be like to actually play Diablo 5.

Chris Wilson, co-creator of Path of Exile and noted Diablo 2 mega fan, has been encouraged by everything Blizzard has shown of Diablo 5, but has one concern based on the messaging so far. Referencing comments from Diablo leadership at this year's BlizzCon suggesting Blizzard is surveying all generations of players from Diablo 1 to 4, Wilson says he's worried Blizzard might be trying to appeal to too many different audiences at once. He points out that Blizzard didn't even label Diablo an action-RPG series until Diablo 2: Lord of Destruction, and that Diablo 3 and 4 each appeal to a different type of player as well.

"This means that when you survey Diablo players and say 'what would you like in a Diablo 5, how can we get you to play it?', you're gonna get many different answers, and I worry that some of these answers might be slightly mutually exclusive," Wilson says in an interview with Destin Legarie. "I'm optimistic by what they showed because there's heavy Diablo 2 signaling, and that's really cool. I just would urge caution, of, it's OK to not appeal to every Diablo player as long as the product that's made is really fun for the core audience you're targeting, and I'm sure they are thinking of the core audience. Like, I'm simplifying it a lot here, but that's my one worry, really, that they go a bit too broad.

"There's a saying, if you make a game for everyone, you make a game for no one," Wilson concludes.

I understand where Wilson's coming from as a fellow Diablo 1+2 diehard, but it seems a little premature to be worrying about a too-safe Diablo 5 based on such limited information. There are all sorts of reasons a developer might survey fans of a series from different entry points, and regardless of Blizzard's reasoning, everything we've seen so far points to the darkest Diablo yet, which if anything stands in stark contrast to a game like Diablo 3. Meanwhile, the aforementioned return to procedural generation and Diablo 2-style itemization further suggests an embrace of the series' roots rather than some broad-strokes appeal to every generation of Diablo player.

This could very well be pure hopium, but the overall vibe I'm getting as a lifelong Diablo player, and as someone who attended this year's BlizzCon and spoken directly with Blizzard, is that the original Diablo is at the forefront of the studio's mind as it works on Diablo 5. To be very, very clear, that's just the collective impression that's formed in my head over dozens of interviews, panels, and videos scanned, and not something I was explicitly told by Blizzard, but it's exactly what I'm hoping for nonetheless.

Diablo 4's nostalgic new season has convinced me that we need a Diablo 1 remake more than Diablo 5

#3832. After gobbling up EA, Saudi Arabia and private equity firm Silver Lake reportedly looking to buy Unity

After acquiring EA for $55bn earlier this year, Saudi Arabia and private equity firm Silver Lake are reportedly in the market for another massive video game company. And according to new reports, it's Unity.

Per Reuters, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and Silver Lake - two major actors in the EA acquisition - are in talks to acquire the video game engine company for around $25bn. Silver Lake's Egon Durban already sits on the Unity Board of Directors, and the firm owns around eight percent of its shares already thanks to a $400m investment.

This $25bn valuation should be taken with a grain of salt for two core reasons. For one, it was decided prior to Unity's latest quarterly financial report, which included a 59% increase in strategic revenue year-over-year and net income of $122m. So this could propel the valuation upwards.

On the other hand, wider economic changes could have a detrimental effect. Reuters points out: "Strong ⁠growth in Unity's AI-powered Vector advertising platform helped it post its first quarterly profit on a GAAP basis since going public in September 2020." Given we've seen the generative AI sector take a major hit this week following the US midterm elections, it's possible companies using the tech may be viewed with more fiscal skepticism. Or, maybe this dip is just temporary. In short, take the $25bn valuation as a ballpark figure.

Unity has had something of an interesting past. There was of course the banana's runtime fee scandal of 2024 in which the company attempted to charge developers a fee on each game sale using the engine, which proved a PR nightmare and was quickly walked back. Unity also recently partnered with Google for AI-game creation platforms Google PlayGround and Unity Spark. Spark is shown to have created a Space Corridor game on its website that looks dubious at best - not exactly a resounding testament to the future.

The last time EA and Silver Lake bought something gaming related it was EA, a Western giant that would go on to lay off hundreds of staff and close BioWare months later. It is worth emphasising that the deal was a leveraged buyout, which saddles EA with substantial debt, whereas the exact nature of this proposed Unity deal is not confirmed. As such if it does happen, it may be a good ol' fashioned private acquisition, not this terms and conditions-laden deal that EA, in its newest guises, must contend with. We've already seen BioWare closed down as a result of this acquisition.

Expect more news about the Unity buyout when official information comes to light.

#3831. How to get Lil’ Uzi Vert Jr. Sprite in Fortnite and how it works

Week 2 of Fortnite Treasure Hunters has added the Lil’ Uzi Vert Sprite to the existing collection, and we can add it to our collection. To do so, however, we have to first collect this Sprite on our runs, and then extract it safely using an Extractor.

Unlike most Sprites in the current season, the Lil’ Uzi Vert Jr. Sprite is a guaranteed drop. However, you’ll have to raid Lil’ Uzi Vert Jr.’s stronghold and outlast the boss battle.

Thankfully, he is one of the easiest bosses to take down. His weapon might do a lot of damage, but not so much if you stay in the shelter and shoot from a distance. Just go for headshots, and you’ll be good to go.

However, you can also end up finding the Cursed or the Fortune variants if you’re lucky enough. The special versions have the same effect as the base version, but they offer an extra modifier.

The Lil’ Uzi Vert Jr. Sprite helps to restore shields of players by triggering a splash effect. This will heal you and your allies. While the move has a cooldown, the time interval can come down once you level up the Sprite. This makes the Sprite one of the best options to consider for team play.

#3830. "Is there any accountability left in this world?" Warren Spector pops off at EA executives and their massive payouts as BioWare shuts down

It's only been two weeks since we last heard Warren Spector sound off about EA's sudden decision to close BioWare, following the publisher's acquisition by Saudi Arabia's PIF and venture capitalist concerns. But now, the storied developer is back and - apparently - angrier than ever.

"I recently posted my thoughts about EA’s shuttering of BioWare," Spector wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "Those of you who read my post know that I was unhappy. I remain so. The tragedy of so many layoffs the last few years hasn’t been lost on me, but for some reason, BioWare hit me on an emotional level that nothing before had. I felt gut-punched."

Spector goes on to counter the idea that the studio was closed down as a "sound business decision" because the "studio’s glory days (artistic and commercial) were behind them" and that "businesses don’t succeed on history alone". These reactions, more than anything else, appear to be what's inspired Spector to take to posting again - he simply cannot agree with this assessment.

"If studio-level people leave, resulting in dilution of talent, someone is creating an environment that pushes them out. Do those culture-killers pay any price? If executives misread the market, over-hire, or make decisions that result in under-funded, over-funded, poorly-marketed games do they lose sleep let alone jobs?" he asks.

"Do those same executives suffer like developers when the needs of financial partners and private investors take precedence over the people who actually create value, let alone over the interests of players? Does anyone up there in or adjacent to the C-suite care? Is there any accountability left in this world? Obviously not."

He then goes on to list the yearly payouts that some of the highest-level executives at EA are rewarded per annum. These include:

"Tens of thousands of do-ers and makers are out of work and these people think they're worth that kind of compensation?" continues Spector. "And if you think this is a discussion about 'sound business decisions', I hope you never get anywhere near running a business. Or at least that people have the sense not to go work for you."

Back in August, we saw Warren Spector announce his intention to retire from the world of video game development. Spector's announcement comes shortly after the last game he worked on - Thick as Thieves - had its final major update only a few months after its release. Despite its charm and low price, Thick as Thieves sadly didn't sell what it needed to, resulting in layoffs at Spector's studio.

#3828. "The lesson learned is you can have both": Skyrim lead designer reckons there's merit in Baldur's Gate 3-style tough choices and Bethesda's do-anything approach

How many doors should be open at any point in an adventure?

Whether RPGs are better off prioritising player freedom or endeavouring to have several doors slam shut every time you put another foot forwards in order to encourage multiple runs with different characters is, to put it bluntly, something I reckon will still be a matter of debate in the year 4000. We'll all have evolved in non-corporeal beings floating in a galaxy that's been racked by such change that even the six million copies of The Elder Scrolls 5 we've littered the Earth with will have been swept away into the great recycling bin on the gods' desktop, and there'll still be sniping going on about whether it's ok that Skyrim lets you be a master thiefssassin who leads the companions, knows every spell under the sun, and slapped up a world-eating dragon for fun.

For what it's worth, the game's lead designer reckons both games that do and don't let you do that have their merits when executed well.

Speaking to The Examined Game, ex-Bethesda dev Bruce Nesmith talked about being "pleasantly surprised" when playing Baldur's Gate 3 just how much he enjoyed making "consequential decisions that closed off gameplay". In Nesmith's view, Larian "redefined things in a certain way" with their take on the D&D universe and the fantasy rules it plays by. However, he argued that there's still merit to taking an approach more akin to Bethesda's post-Morrowind Elder Scrolls entries and striving to make it possible for the player to see the majority of what the game has to offer in a single playthrough.

"They were both fun," he said. "They were just fun in different ways and that to me was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things that you couldn't have both [of]. The lesson learned is you can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

Nesmith made clear that he still thinks the idea of, with a few exceptions like Skyrim's civil war, not gating the player off from the likes of doing multiple faction questlines is a "very good philosophy" that he supports.

As much as it's always a bit of a cop out to declare that everything's equally good, actually, I do think that there's merit in both approaches. I love the dedication the likes of New Vegas, Disco Elysium, and The Witcher 2 have to making you pick a path and see where it takes you at the expense of not seeing other stuff. Hell, the latter game's infamous for being totally different depending on who you choose to waltz off with at the end of the opening act.

That said, Skyrim's open-endedness was undoubtedly one of the factors which made it so easy for me to get majorly into when I was just cutting my teeth in RPGs as a teenager. There's value in such games existing, even if for plenty it might be as a gateway drug to games with crunchier and more challenging narratives that do demand you plug in your brain and carefully consider every choice you make. Whether there's still as much value in being the gateway drug nowadays compared to in 2011 is the question The Elder Scrolls 6'll likely answer whenever it rocks up. Coming as it is after the likes of BG3 and The Witcher 3 have had near Skyrim-level gangbusters success while leaning a lot more heavily into the hard stuff typically pegged as having less potential for mass appeal.

For what it's worth, while you can very much argue about the execution, Fallout 4's main quest was a lot more choice-heavy than Fallout 3's. So, Bethesda may well opt to pivot or make compromises in their player freedom-first ways if they feel some crunchier choice is in order.

On a recent visit to Jackbox Games HQ here in Chicago, I got to speak with developers and studio leadership about their process, history, and place in the industry. Given, you know, everything, I'm pretty much contractually obligated to ask about AI in conversations like this. Here's what CEO Mike Bilder had to say on the topic:

"The people are what make this product. The comedy, the writing, and the art, all that is done by people, and we have no intention of changing that. I don't think we're experts on what's going on with AI in the industry and any of that. There's obviously uses for tooling and for research, and [for] all that kind of stuff [AI is] incredibly powerful.

"But from a generative asset standpoint, we don't have any intention of replacing people, or people-made editorial and art with it."

From everything we had discussed up to this point, as well as Jackbox's whole deal, I didn't think generative AI would really be in the cards for the studio. But I still appreciated Bilder's straightforward, clear answer on the subject, particularly when the standard playbook these days is fence sitting reminiscent of The Simpsons' "Abortions for some, miniature American flags for others."

Jackbox's games are relatively lightweight from a tech perspective, while the art and writing is their main draw⁠—if anything was noticeably AI-generated, it would put the value of the whole package into question.

The company recently released the Jackbox Party Pack 12 on October 14, and the studio's production values have really progressed since the last entry I had played⁠—Trivia Murder Party 3 makes extensive use of realtime 3D graphics, for example. Jackbox Party Pack 12 is available on pretty much everything, but this is Personal Computer Gamer, so I'll say you can grab it on Steam.

#3826. Former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect to curb AI clones

Former Rockstar Games North technical director Obbe Vermeij believes that the possibility of AI vibe coded ports of Grand Theft Auto 6 could push Rockstar to create an official PC version sooner than you'd expect.

Speaking to RockPaperShotgun as part of a wider interview, Vermeij said generative AI "really has changed the world.". He elaborated: "I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC, which won't be as good as [the developer's] effort, but it could still also hurt their sales. We've already seen people thrust footage of Grand Theft Auto 6 into AI software over the past few months. Grand Theft Auto 6 itself will not feature any generative AI or microtransactions at launch.

AI game clones continue to be a problem. Game developers have cancelled public demos in fear of having their game copied, and Steam owner Valve has gone out to say it's the developer's responsibility to prevent cloning by making their games more original. Even as Anthropic has introduced measures to prevent such practices, other AI software can still perform such tasks.

#3825. Microsoft workers accuse company of trying to get customers "addicted" to AI while forcing it on their own staff and making them party to "human rights violations"

Open letter warns of "a cascade of business and ethics risks"

A group of "concerned Microsoft workers" have published an open letter criticising their employer's "speed-at-all-costs" approach to generative AI, which they argue is "harming our customers, colleagues, shareholders, vendors, and the planet". They accuse Microsoft leadership of trying to get people "addicted" to genAI, while making their own staff miserable by mandating AI usage.

Echoing the on-going BDS campaign against Microsoft's Xbox business, the writers contend that Microsoft have become party to "human rights violations" by selling generative AI technology to Israel's military during the latter's invasion of Gaza, which a UN commission has deemed a genocide. They're also critical of Microsoft's contracts with the USA's draconian Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. While seemingly not against generative AI in principle, they're organising against "the AI industry’s trajectory to continue to enrich AI’s powerful few", pointing out that AI companies now account for a terrifying share of the global stock market.

I know about the letter thanks to Vertical Slice, who cite a New York Times report on Microsoft's recent voluntary buyouts, which follow several waves of mass layoffs at a company with a market value of around $4 trillion.

"For many, working at Microsoft has become joyless and demoralizing, with job satisfaction declining around the same time the company accelerated its AI investments," the workers write. "Crushing workloads, threats of AI job replacement and layoffs, constantly shifting business priorities, and re-orgs destabilize our work environment and erode employee trust in leadership."

The letter organisers complain that "workers are forced to use AI in almost every work area, with little to no training and no strategic rationale besides 'speed'," obliging them to spend a lot of time "learning and relearning tools, fixing AI slop, and reworking or rolling back low-quality features". They feel that Microsoft's generative AI strategy is exposing customers "to overreliance, misuse, and physical and mental harm", not least because "our own research shows that AI agents don’t prioritize user safety, and internal planning documents detail how to 'make people addicted' to AI products." If that last part is an actual quote from an internal feature document, then: yeeeeeeesh.

The writers further take issue with Microsoft's investments in data centers for generative AI use, which may use up a lot of water while contributing to carbon emissions (jeopardising Microsoft's older commitments to reducing their carbon footprint). They note that "our Community-First AI Infrastructure plan makes vague financial and job-creation commitments, but doesn’t address greenhouse gas emissions or other damage already being done."

The organisers also call out their employer for becoming "a partner to human rights violations" by licensing generative AI tools to the Israeli military and ICE. "Not only are we risking reputational, financial, and legal damage, we are allowing our AI products to be used against whole communities for mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, and genocide," they write.

Finally, they take a swing at "Microsoft’s participation in circular investment across a handful of AI leaders " - that is, AI companies pouring cash into each other, which naturally creates the risk of several companies biting the dust if one company's fortunes take a tumble. This ouroboros strategy "exposes workers, customers, shareholders, and society to a cascade of business and ethics risks," the writers claim, noting that AI-linked stocks now dominate the S&P 500 index.

The letter writers have a number of demands. They'd like more say over "AI product strategy decisions", and for Microsoft to consider customer feedback and bring different development disciplines together "to help guard against shipping AI-worsened user experiences". They want Microsoft to "offer quality training and empower workers to integrate AI in their workflows without tying AI use to rewards, reprimand or layoffs." They call on the execs to "end unfair AI-driven workforce reductions and agree to worker protections".

Looking beyond Microsoft's walls, the workers argue that "job opportunities from data center investments are mostly temporary" and that "Microsoft must protect all workers, not attempt to avoid the unionized trades in local communities, and ensure a just transition for all impacted workers."

The letter writers call on Microsoft to "expand Responsible AI and Sensitive Use teams and fund programs to communicate potential harms to users". They would like Microsoft to stop selling AI materials to organisations "if they are engaged in violence, mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, or genocide", requesting that Microsoft "transparently share contracts with all governments and their agencies or contractors, including police and armed forces, and immediately terminate any contracts with those directly or indirectly involved in human rights violations."

The letter writers want Microsoft to "reduce financial dependency on OpenAI and other AI partners and provide transparency into all AI investments". In general, they want their bosses to "stop offloading financial risk to workers, vendors, partners, customers, and shareholders through irresponsible investments and relationships." As regards the environment, the workers are demanding that Microsoft "reaffirm our goal to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste by 2030". They want Microsoft to cooperate more with environmental regulators, and "to respect local communities by rejecting dirty energy, engaging fairly and transparently, and refusing to build in resource-scarce areas."

It's not clear who, exactly, is behind the letter, or how many others at Microsoft have signed as of writing. I've requested comment from Microsoft, and will update this piece as and when I hear more.

Hollow Knight: Silksong has a new physical edition, and early arrivals reveal a surprise message from developer Team Cherry regarding additional content coming to the game in the months and, seemingly, years ahead.

Metroidvania marketing man Matthew Griffin reminds fans that "Hollow Knight: Silksong (Standard Edition) is arriving soon on November 10th." It comes with a user manual, a hand-drawn map, and reversible cover art. We're most interested in that user manual, which ends with a section on "Content Packs," per images shared online by fans who got their physical copy a smidge early.

"The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," this page of the manual reads. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!"

The plurality of this promise is what's raised some eyebrows. After the many DLCs Hollow Knight received, there was little doubt that Team Cherry would add a truckload of content to Silksong. This is not a studio known for restraint. But how would all those ideas be expressed? Official word of several "free content packs" containing multiple "new abilities" for protagonist Hornet has predictably excited fans.

The manual continues: "In the first giant expansion, voyage across and beneath a salt-stricken ocean brimming with mystery and menace." Here again, fans linger on this being the first giant expansion for Silksong.

Hollow Knight also got multiple DLC packs – Hidden Dreams, The Grimm Troupe, Lifeblood, and Godmaster – adding bosses, items, areas, storylines, and exacting arena challenges. Previous comments from developers Ari Gibson and William Pellen suggested Silksong may receive a similar variety of additional content, with Sea of Sorrow expected to be a Grimm Troupe-like shotgun blast of experiences.

The manual concludes with a Hollow Knight: Silksong - Sea of Sorrow emblem that reads, "Coming soon." You'll note that this, like everything else Team Cherry has said, doesn't say when soon is.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Last year, Team Cherry announced Sea of Sorrow and charted a 2026 launch. Apart from a February update on a port for the original Hollow Knight and a March post confirming expanded Silksong language support, the studio hasn't said anything else on its blog or social feeds all year. Pellen previously said Team Cherry would be more communicative, and we can see how that panned out. Three blog posts in a year, dare we dream?

In a read that's only slightly generous, it's possible that this blank phrasing, used in place of a definitive release date, is just generalist wording or an artifact of this physical edition's production. Maybe Team Cherry didn't want to announce anything major in such a limited product. But this does read like a step back from the 2026 target in the expansion's reveal trailer.

Team Cherry is quiet and spontaneous enough that a Sea of Sorrow shadow drop, or at least a release date with very little notice, wouldn't surprise me. Silksong's launch also came out of nowhere, giving countless other games just two weeks to flee the blast radius. But 2026 is rapidly coming to a close and we haven't heard a peep from Team Cherry about the expansion, so I also wouldn't be surprised if this manual does, as players fear, herald a delay into 2027.

Recent YouTube comments on Sea of Sorrow's trailer tell the whole story. "Team Cherry...? Where are you...?" wonders one viewer.

The vibes are very similar to those around The Duskbloods, a Nintendo Switch 2-exclusive FromSoftware game long said to be releasing in 2026. As the months flew by without any official word, a delay seemed more and more likely, though FromSoftware also notably had some negative test feedback to respond to. Lo and behold, The Duskbloods was delayed. But much like FromSoftware, Team Cherry can pretty much do what it wants, when it wants, and millions of fans will show up anyway.

#3822. Following BioWare's shock closure, a new documentary capturing its final moments is coming next year

A documentary detailing the history of beloved Mass Effect studio BioWare is releasing next year, and will cover last month's shock closure of the studio, following the private acquisition of owner EA.

Mass Effect: The BioWare Story (per Deadline) has been written and directed by Akash Sherman and produced for Canada's Super Channel. It documents the studio from the early days after its founding in 1995 to the release of barn-burner hits like Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Filming began two years prior to the announcement of BioWare's closure and continued throughout, with Deadline reporting the documentary will "capture BioWare’s final chapter."

The BioWare Story includes interviews with studio founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk, and Augustine Yip, alongside Mass Effect director Casey Hudson, other BioWare developers, and Shepard voice actor Jennifer Hale. That's alongside former EA CEO John Riccitiello, LucasFilm Games vice president Douglas Reilly, and creator of The Game Awards Geoff Keighley.

"The BioWare founders are my hometown heroes,” writer and director Sherman said in a statement accompanying the documentary news. "It's a privilege and responsibility to share the journey of underdogs who came together to create deeply beloved storytelling. Their golden era kindled a spark in me and in an entire generation. With the studio's recent closure, the film is now a profound valediction."

For fans outside Canada, Mass Effect: The BioWare Story is planned for a major film festival run and a world premiere next year. No exact release date has been established as of writing.

Members of the games industry have lambasted EA's decision to close Bioware in the weeks since the news was shared, with legendary designer Warren Spector writing, "Anyone who participated in this travesty should be ashamed". Meanwhile, a petition has reached enough signatures for the Canadian government to potentially rescue the studio from closure. Whether or not it actually does… Well, weirder things have happened?

#3821. Cyberattack on Sega third-party newsletter distributor reportedly sees over two million email addresses leaked, but Sega accounts unaffected

Japanese email distribution firm Arara were the target of the attack

Sega have revealed that over two million email addresses have leaked due to a cyberattack on Japanese email delivery provider Arara, whom the Like A Dragon and Sonic publishers use to distribute newsletters. Sega and Arara are currently busy investigating what happened in the breach, which doesn't appear to have affected the Sega accounts you can use receive in-game rewards and access a calendar which reminds you when it's Kazuma Kiryu's birthday. The companies have urged those who signed up for the affected newsletters to be wary of potential phishing attempts.

According to Automaton, who've translated Sega's official press release about the cyberattack, 2,196,044 email addresses in total were affected. 92,273 of that number were linked to the newsletter distribution.

The company have listed some specific newsletter releases as having been affected, including two exhibition announcements for this year's Tokyo Game Show, the announcement of arcade rhythm game Chunithm Mate's launch, six newsletters about online character lottery service Sega Lucky Kuji Online, the launch of a rhythm game update dubbed Ongeki Re:Fresh Act.2, and the launch of another arcade rhythm game update called Maimai DX MAGiCAL. Number one, that's a lot of rhythm games, and number two, Sega have advised those who opted in and received those newsletters to watch out for fishing emails from people posing as being tied to Sega or Arara.

Sega reportedly confirmed that - as far as the affected emails go - no names, dates of birth, genders, residential addresses, phone numbers, credit card information, and passwords are known to have been leaked. There had also been no reports of cases where the leaked information had been misused as of the time Sega made their announcement. The company have naturally put distributing any further email newsletters through Arara on hold until their investigation's done and plan to reach out to each affected person individually once the full details of the leak have been confirmed.

While data breaches and cyberattacks are nothing new, there have been a fair few recently, with both Street Fighter makers Capcom and Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 devs Warhorse suffering incidents of their own last month.

#3818. Swarmbreaker is an uncommonly mesmerising tower defence game in which enemies "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid"

It is said that King Canute once placed his throne on the shore and commanded the sea not to get his feet wet, thus proving to his flattering courtiers that only God Almighty holds sway over the elements. "But sire!" I would have told him, if I'd been one of the aforesaid lickspittles. "Why not lay down spike strips and park a couple of flamethrowers in the shallows?" I would have said this because I have just been playing Swarmbreaker, a tower defence game that aims to prove there is no fluid body so awe-inspiring that it cannot be machine-gunned into submission.

In Swarmbreaker - which launches on Steam tomorrow, and still has a demo as of writing – you have to defend your rocketship against waves of insect aggressors, who spawn at the map's far corners. Between waves, you spend earnings from kills on turrets, barricades, troops, and upgrades for all the foregoing. Sounds like bog-standard attrition management, perhaps, but what lifts Swarmbreaker is the "swarm" part. The rapacious scuttlers come in several distinct varieties, but they also "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid".

The results are hypnotic: coloured particles burst from each burrow and course through the map's contours, pushing movable terrain elements and eroding your structures like acid. You can practically hear the oil derricks fizz as they are engulfed and chewed to a lumpy puddle of iridescent digestive enzymes. Speaking of which, the more oil derricks you save during each wave, the more cash you'll have to spend before the next, but committing to their protection obviously risks leaving your ship exposed. Your fallback option is an inexhaustible mouse-click-fired artillery cannon, but this won't save you if the bulk of the swarm makes it all the way to your doorstep.

I'm still not convinced this isn't a run-of-the-mill tower defender, beneath it all, but it's worth giving the demo a shot just to enjoy the swirling tidal dynamics of homocidal buglife. What would King Canute have made of it all? I think he would have stuck his throne right by the biggest burrow, surrounded by gravity traps and howitzers. "Back in your hole, hungry liquids!" he'd have bellowed, firing dual AK47s simultaneously. "The only god I recognise is efficient chokepoint management! Death to sense-of-flow! Death to trickle-down politics!"

"SIRE," I'd have told him sternly. "You are getting your metaphors confused. And also that is a total waste of howitzers - those things are best placed on hills." Read more on Steam.

#3817. Square Enix accidentally botches a Nier: Automata update, balloons required file size from 50GB to 366GB on PC

"Do you think games are silly little things?"

Yesterday, Nier: Automata received a new patch on Steam, adding more language support to the title - it can now be played with Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese options - but this new update also, somehow, inflated the file size of the game on PC from about 50GB to 366GB. D'oh! What's worse is, the update is not optional.

The cause of this, reportedly, is a bug that caused all the DLC in the YoRHa Edition of the game to become the same size as the base game - and the new download stacks them all concurrently. "Only SquareEnix can turn 40GB into 366GB with 8GB patch," says one dissatisfied Steam reviewer.

If you don't have space for this massive new file on your PC (and I can't say I blame you, it's ridiculous), there is a workaround, as confirmed by Square Enix in a tweet via its Japanese Twitter account.

"We have confirmed an issue where, following the latest update to the Steam version of Nier: Automata, the installation process indicates that more storage space is required than expected," noted the publisher. "We are currently investigating the cause and working on a solution. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. As a temporary workaround, you can download the base game by unchecking the DLC under Steam → Properties → DLC."

It's quite ironic, really, that so many Steam reviewers are complaining about things like "I just need to delete 90% of my computer to install this" when a large part of the game is managing the software/programmes installed on your android protagonists in order to upgrade your abilities and stats. There's even an ending for uninstalling your OS on your mechanical main characters. I'd be inclined to suggest this is some sort of meta psy-op from creator Yoko Taro, but… nah, that's just fantasy, isn't it? Isn't it?

Speaking of Taro, earlier this year we learned that "Nier Automata will continue", though we only heard back in 2025 that most of the projects the developer was working on were cancelled. One of these may have been the Tencent-backed Nier mobile game in 2024, which reportedly "struggled to find a monetisation to offset its high costs."

The final trailer for Prime Video’s Blade Runner 2099 has arrived, and it's the end of the world as we know it.

In the brief clip, which can be viewed above, Replicants have taken over Los Angeles and are killing humans in broad daylight. Cora (Hunter Schafer) is humanity's last hope, as she volunteers to go undercover as a Blade Runner who is overseen by Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant who is in the final weeks of her life.

"It's harder to look something in the eye than to kill it," Olwen says over a montage of dreary neo-futuristic violence. Another voice assures someone, most likely someone human, that what Cora's doing will "make the world ours again." Given how bleak things are, I'm not so sure. Created by Silka Luisa and executive-produced by Ridley Scott, the cast includes Dimitri Abold, Amy Lennox, Lewis Gribben, and Wil Coban. It's worth noting that, although Scott worked pretty closely with Luisa on the making of the series, Blade Runner 2099 is meant to be its own eight-episode standalone limited series... and that Ryan Gosling's K won't be popping up in a cameo or anything of that nature.

If this is the first you've heard of Dark Heresy, here's Owlcat's synopsis of what it's all about:

Embrace the role of an Inquisitor in the grim darkness of the far future in a cRPG set in the rich Warhammer 40,000 universe. Start your service as an acolyte of the Inquisition: Investigate heresy, command a diverse warband, and shape the fate of the Calixis Sector in a story-rich experience where every decision has weight, justice is non-existent, and the line between salvation and damnation is razor-thin. Explore an in-depth depiction of the Inquisition as an organisation and the vast force it commands: its power, bureaucracy, and inner conflicts laid bare like never before.

As an Inquisitor, you have one primary goal: to protect the Imperium, whether that be from the taint of xenos, the betrayal of heretics, or the scourge of mutants, by any means necessary. #3814. All Fortnite Treasure Hunters loot odds and drop rates explained – Pirate Shop, Weekly Gold Outfit, and more

In Fortnite Treasure Hunters, there’s quite a vast collection of special loot you can find and permanently add to your collection. This includes special Treasure Chest items, which have been revealed to have specific odds and drop rates.

The hunt for these rare assets is quite tough and time-consuming, so if you’re unsure whether it’s worth keeping at it, reviewing the specific statistics for acquiring each item may help make this decision easier. Here are all loot odds and drop rates for Treasure Chest items like the Pirate Shop Access, Weekly Gold Outfit, and more in Fortnite Treasure Hunters.

The odds and drop rates for each item you can find in Treasure Chests around the Fortnite Treasure Hunters island vary, with the Weekly Gold Outfit and Pirate Shop Access having the overall lowest numbers. The official statistics for all items were shared on the Fortnite Status page on X (formerly Twitter), so here’s a complete breakdown of all of them.

These base stats apply to all featured weekly Treasure Chest loot and reward items throughout the entire season. Each week, you can only get one of each type of treasure, except for Gizmos.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Each time you open a chest in Fortnite Treasure Hunters, there’s a chance you may find one of the special Treasure Chest loot items. Whether or not you find one of these items is essentially RNG and comes down to random luck landing in your favor.

For example, when opening a chest, your odds of acquiring the Weekly Gold Outfit are the worst, with only a 1 in 1,562,500 chance (about 0.000064 percent) of finding this item. For Gizmos, on the other hand, the drop rates look a lot better, with a 1 in 127 (about 0.787 percent) chance of acquiring one while looting.

Technically, the more you loot, the more shots you have at finding these rare items. Opening more chests does not increase your odds or guarantee you will eventually find what you’re seeking, but the more you do try, the more chances you have of getting lucky.

All drop rates and odds for Treasure Chest loot items consistently stay the same throughout every day of the season. Nothing causes them to drop or get lower. The only changes you’ll ever see to these rates are special, helpful boosts to the odds that occur during Treasure Hour events.

During special Treasure Hour events, Treasure Chest loot has boosted drop rates, making all of these assets a bit easier to find. The base boosted odds of finding these items are:

The base boosted drop rates apply to most standard events that increase these stats, but these odds may also sometimes vary a bit to be slightly better depending on the specific theme of the Treasure Hour event. To see exactly what the altered boosted rate of all items is during any of these events, you can either check the official Fortnite Status page on X (formerly Twitter) or view the game announcement while the event is live.

If you need a break from hunting for treasure, there are plenty of other tasks to keep you busy around the island. Next, you might consider working on getting the Sweet Dreams Sprite, contacting Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port, and unlocking all Captain X rewards.

#3813. World of Warcraft: Forever hotfix puts a stop to super speedy flag carriers that were dominating PvP battlegrounds

World of Warcraft: Forever has received its first major hotfix patch, which among other things has put an end to an especially powerful bug that made PvP battlegrounds like Warsong Gulch favoured to the Horde's advantage.

While Taurens are running, they gradually build up stacks of increased movement speed. They gain a two percent movement speed bonus per stack, and it stacks up to 30 times. That means a Tauren can gain 60 percent increased movement speed, though it's worth noting that when they stop moving, these stacks decrease. In short, cows run fast.

The Hotfix, detailed in this Blizzard blog post, stops the Tauren's plainsrunning passive from stacking during a battleground's preparation phase. What players were doing to exploit this was running back and forth in the minutes before the Warsong Gulch battleground let both teams loose. It's a capture the flag game mode, so once the gates opened, Taurens were sprinting ahead of everyone else, allowing them to quickly push towards the enemy base for a potential early flag capture.

In addition, the hotfix removes any plainsrunning stacks from Taurens once they pick up the enemy flag, and prevents them from gaining stacks while the flag is in their possession. The goal of the enemy team is to stop and kill the enemy flag carrier as soon as possible, so a Tauren moving far faster than any of your team made this pretty difficult.

Tauren's could be tanky warriors or druids too, which further added to the difficulty in killing them. With this change they're now easier to lock down, though it's worth noting a Tauren can still make use of Plainsrunning to rush into the enemy base early. They just don't have that wild speed boost from the jump.

Surely this was the only reason my Alliance Warsong Gulch games were all lost this morning, and not because my faction is for chumps. In other World of Warcraft: Forever news, the launch earlier this week was applauded as one of the smoothest in the series history, save for a few broken boats and zeppelins.

The hotfix has also decreased the respawn time of the NPC Deathstalker Erland who is needed for an escort quest. People were mulling around his spawn and wasting away while waiting for him to respawn. Also, supply vendors on the Zephras Isle have been stocked with handy tradeskill bags that you could find in other starter zones. It's the shipping I assume, it takes a while for stock to make it all the way up there.

Maybe laying off people who know what they're doing is bad, actually.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I don't know about you, but I'm not a huge fan of the way YouTube encourages everything becoming a video that's over an hour long and doesn't have a text version available. There's a recent video putting the original Pool of Radiance into the greater context of the history of CRPGs that's almost 10 hours long, and the odds of me watching more than 10% of it are perishingly low.

Fortunately for you, we're here to convert video to text for your edification, as with The Examined Game's comprehensive interview with Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith. Asked how a game as successful as Skyrim came to be, Nesmith emphasized the importance of keeping the team together.

If I had an actual blueprint on how to do it, I would be one rich son of a bitch. A lot of it comes down to we had the same team that had worked on Oblivion. The studio had not really changed dramatically. So we were able to deal with institutional knowledge at a high level that had been retained, which allows us to not make mistakes and build on successes. That was definitely key to it.

I think also we gave a high priority to making sure that the world was full. There was nowhere that you went where there wasn't at least something fun to see if not something fun to do. And it and it can be just little things, it can be a little vignette on the side of the road. It doesn't have to be a huge big adventure, but the visual storytelling was fantastic.

I go back to that sense of freedom once again, but we accelerated that in Skyrim compared to Oblivion. It makes the world feel rich when there's a variety of experiences. The same experience over and over and over again doesn't cut it. So you have a wealth of enemy types, you've got a lot of different treasure types and loot types, you're allowed to pick everything up in the world.

I have to disagree with Nesmith on the characters, because memorable NPCs are one of Skyrim's weak spots—all those people with recycled voices and limited dialogue. But he's right that Skyrim feels full despite the absence of Ubisoft-style repeatable activities. At no point do you pick up a butterfly and get a notification that says "1/100 butterflies collected". The butterflies are just there, and you can grab them and turn them into potion ingredients if you want. Then while you're out harvesting ingredients you meet a thief or a dying orc or an NPC who points you to a sidequest, and you're off on a new journey. That's what Skyrim does well.

Nesmith goes on to say depth like that was made possible, "by having people who knew what they were doing and could hit the ground running. You didn't have to train people what it meant to make an Elder Scrolls game." Instead of laying off half the Oblivion team the moment it shipped, Bethesda kept them together. "If you look at the history of AAA studios that do sequels, you'll see that repeated," Nesmith continues. "You'll see the best game in a sequence frequently was able to maintain a particular percentage of the staff—was able to maintain a vision."

#3811. Bringing Bloodborne back is tricky because "there's a lot of involved rights associated," according to former PlayStation boss

Every year, Bloodborne fans pray for the birth of another game set in FromSoftware's Lovecraftian world. Every year, we're no closer to a Bloodborne 2 or even a Bloodborne Remastered. But why? PlayStation's former head honcho, Shawn Layden, blames it on the tricky situation of rights ownership.

Asked about the noticeable lack of Bloodborne in the decade since its blood moon shone down on us all, in an interview with The Trophy Room podcast, Layden explained that returning to any beloved game is tough.

"Bringing back old games has a certain challenge to it," he said. "Can you do something that is not only respectful of the original, but can you, you know, recreate the phenomenon as it were?"

Bloodborne's situation is slightly more complicated, though. It seems that the rights are somehow split between original publisher PlayStation, developer FromSoftware and the studio's primary stakeholder Kadokawa Corporation.

"There's a lot of involved rights associated with it, and in something like that - where Sony's in there and [FromSoftware] is in there and From's parent company is in there - I think just getting everyone to sign off on the same thing is probably the biggest challenge there," Layden said.

Having led the PlayStation brand during most of its PS4 golden years, Layden said working with FromSoftware on Bloodborne and the original Demon's Souls was "fantastic."

Despite endless calls for a comeback and very stable sales more than a decade on, Bloodborne itself is still stuck on the PS4 - though it's still playable via backward compatibility on the PS5, I should add. The closest we seemingly got to a Bloodborne comeback came from Bluepoint Games, which reportedly pitched a remake sometime before parent company PlayStation shut down the acclaimed studio, though FromSoftware supposedly didn't want the project to go ahead.

Another former PlayStation executive, Shuhei Yoshida, previously speculated that Bloodborne hasn't been remade because game director and soulslike pioneer, Hidetaka Miyazaki, would prefer to handle it himself: "Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created… So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."

Elsewhere, a Bloodborne animated feature is in the works with YouTuber JackSepticEye attached as a co-producer.

The company wants to "capture institutional knowledge" before it's too late

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo of America is one of many companies investing in game preservation, and a new job listing gives us some insight into what those efforts look like. The company is looking to hire a "digital archivist" to build a library of historical material that can last for generations.

"We are seeking a Digital Archivist, Historical Systems to support the preservation, organization, and accessibility of historical hardware and software information," the company says in its job listing. "This role will design and implement a structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms."

That's a lot of technical words for a position that ultimately boils down to 'build an internal library.' A company like Nintendo of America may have vast piles of historical development documents, advertising materials, and software prototypes on hand, but if nobody knows where any individual thing can be located, it may as well be lost altogether.

While many players might hear the phrase "game preservation" and think of efforts to ensure games are playable on modern devices, the field is far broader than that. Organizations like the Video Game History Foundation specialize in preserving not individual games, but development documents and other historical ephemera providing context on how historical games were developed, released, and played in their time.

Game publishers are starting to invest in this area themselves. PlayStation has a vast vault of historical materials, and Blizzard is building the same sort of archive. For the most part, these archives are never intended to be viewed by the public, but their work can help developers looking to build on historical games. Archived materials might, for example, show up as bonus features in remastered games.

Nintendo's digital archivist "will establish standards and processes that ensure historical information remains discoverable, usable, and preserved for future generations." The company describes this as a 12-month contract position, so it's presumably hoping that its hire will set up an archive and workflow that employees can then add to autonomously.

Perhaps the most notable duty in the job listing is this: "Interview subject matter experts and long-tenured employees to capture institutional knowledge." Nintendo's made a point of hanging onto longtime staff even as other companies lay off developers with decades of experience, but even in an environment that values experience many of gaming's most notable developers are reaching retirement age. Saving their stories and experience for the next generation is going to be a massive boon.

#3808. Mass Effect-like RPG The Expanse: Osiris Reborn ropes in David Gaider, the original lead writer of Bioware's Dragon Age series

"Focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative."

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn looks like it's carrying the best bits of Mass Effect forward, and in an encouraging move, the developers have been collaborating with David Gaider.

Of course, David Gaider is best known as the lead writer on Dragon Age: Origins, Dragon Age 2 and Dragon Age: Inquisition - he's also often credited as the architect of its dark fantasy world Thedas. Gaider's post-BioWare career saw him open his own game development house Summerfall Studios, which most recently released an ambitious roleplaying musical called Stray Gods.

But he's now lending a hand to a game that's not too dissimilar to BioWare's other hugely famous roleplaying series, while still working on his own games at Summerfall.

"Alongside my work at Summerfall, I've also been collaborating with the Owlcat Games team on The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative. The Expanse has long been one of my favourite series, and so obviously I jumped at the opportunity to be involved," he wrote on BlueSky.

"The Owlcat team has been so great, it's really such a treat. One thing I enjoy is how responsive they are to the fans," Gaider added, pointing to how the studio recently recast the male version of its protagonist in response to feedback. The game's reworked and re-designed Martian Captain is now voiced by Blythe Melin.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn shouldn't be confused for the other very Mass Effect-y RPG coming out next year, Exodus. Though it's good to hear that both upcoming projects have some BioWare veterans on board, especially after the famed developer was shut down and had its own promising, actual Mass Effect game cancelled.

Bertie enjoyed what he played of the upcoming game in Eurogamer's The Expanse preview, but also had some concerns about the developer's use of generative AI.
